beads.greek: LIBER TERTIUS [3.pr.1] Delphicus Apollo Socratem omnium sapientissimum Pythiae responsis est professus.
beads.english: BOOK THREE [3.pr.1] Delphic Apollo, through the responses of the Pythia, declared Socrates the wisest of all men.

beads.greek: is autem memoratur prudenter doctissimeque dixisse, oportuisse hominum pectora fenestrata et aperta esse, uti non occultos haberent sensus sed patentes ad considerandum.
beads.english: He, moreover, is recorded to have said, prudently and most learnedly, that the breasts of men ought to have been furnished with windows and open, so that they might hold their thoughts not hidden but laid open for examination.

beads.greek: utinam vero rerum natura sententiam eius secuta explicata et apparentia ea constituisset!
beads.english: Would indeed that the nature of things, following his opinion, had established them unfolded and visible!

beads.greek: si enim ita fuisset, non solum laudes aut vitia animorum ad manum aspicerentur, sed etiam disciplinarum scientiae sub oculorum consideratione subiectae non incertis iudiciis probarentur, sed et doctis et scientibus auctoritas egregia et stabilis adderetur ipsique artifices pellicerent sua prudentia, qui, etiam si non pecunia sint copiosi seu vetustate officinarum habuerint notitiam aut etiam gratia forensi et eloquentia, cum fuerint parati, pro industria studiorum auctoritates possent habere, ut eis, quod profitentur scire, id crederetur.
beads.english: For if it had been so, not only would the merits or vices of minds be seen close at hand, but also the knowledge of the disciplines, placed under the scrutiny of the eyes, would be tested not by uncertain judgements; rather, an outstanding and stable authority would be added to the learned and the knowledgeable, and the craftsmen themselves would win favour by their own expertise, who, even if they are not abundant in money, or have not acquired renown through the long standing of their workshops, or even through influence in the forum and eloquence, yet, when they are well prepared, could possess authority in proportion to the diligence of their studies, so that what they profess to know would be believed of them.

beads.greek: igitur quoniam haec non ita, sed uti natura rerum voluit, sunt constituta, non efficitur, ut possint homines obscuratis sub pectoribus ingeniis scientias artificiorum penitus latentes, quemadmodum sint, iudicare.
beads.english: Therefore, since these matters have been established not thus, but as the nature of things has willed, it does not come about that men are able to judge, with talents obscured beneath the breast, how the sciences of the crafts, lying deeply hidden, really are.

beads.greek: [3.pr.2] Maxime autem id animadvertere possumus ab antiquis statuariis et pictoribus, quod ex his, qui dignitatis notas et commendationis gratiam habuerunt, aeterna memoria ad posteritatem sunt permanentes, uti Myron, Polycletus, Phidias, Lysippus ceterique, qui nobilitatem ex arte sunt consecuti.
beads.english: [3.pr.2] But we can observe this most of all from the ancient sculptors and painters, because of these, those who possessed the marks of distinction and the favour of recommendation remain in everlasting memory for posterity, such as Myron, Polyclitus, Phidias, Lysippus and the rest, who attained renown from their art.

beads.greek: namque ut civitatibus magnis aut regibus aut civibus nobilibus opera fecerunt, ita id sunt adepti.
beads.english: For as they made works for great cities or for kings or for noble citizens, so they attained this.

beads.greek: at qui non minore studio et ingenio sollertiaque fuerunt nobilibus et humili fortuna civibus non minus egregie perfecta fecerunt opera, nullam memoriam sunt adsecuti, quod hi non ab industria neque artis sollertia sed a felicitate fuerunt deserti, ut Hegias Atheniensis, Chion Corinthius, Myagrus Phocaeus, Pharax Ephesius, Boedas Byzantius etiamque alii plures.
beads.english: But those who, with no less devotion and talent and skill, made works no less excellently finished for citizens of noble (nobilibus) and of humble fortune, have obtained no memory at all, because these were abandoned not by industry nor by skill in their art but by good fortune, such as Hegias of Athens, Chion of Corinth, Myagrus of Phocaea, Pharax of Ephesus, Boedas of Byzantium and also several others.

beads.greek: non minus item pictores, uti Aristomenes Thasius, Polycles et Androcydes Cyzice ni, Theo Magnes ceterique, quos neque industria neque artis studium neque sollertia defecit, sed aut rei familiaris exiguitas aut inbecillitas fortunae seu in ambitione certationis contrariorum superatio obstitit eorum dignitati.
beads.english: Likewise no less the painters, such as Aristomenes of Thasos, Polycles and Androcydes of Cyzicus, Theo of Magnesia and the rest, whom neither industry nor devotion to the art nor skill failed, but either the slenderness of their family estate or the weakness of their fortune or their being overcome by rivals in the canvassing of competition stood in the way of their distinction.

beads.greek: [3.pr.3] Nec tamen est admirandum, si propter ignotitiam artis virtutes obscurantur, sed maxime indignandum, cum etiam saepe eblandiatur gratia conviviorum a veris iudiciis falsam probationem.
beads.english: [3.pr.3] And yet it is not to be wondered at if, through ignorance of the art, its excellences are obscured; but it is most to be resented when, as often happens, the favour won at dinner-parties even coaxes a false approval away from true judgements.

beads.greek: ergo, uti Socrati placuit, si ita sensus et sententiae scientiaeque disciplinis auctae perspicuae et perlucidae fuissent, non gratia neque ambitio valeret, sed si qui veris certisque laboribus doctrinarum pervenissent ad scientiam summam, eis ultro opera traderentur.
beads.english: Therefore, as Socrates held, if perceptions and opinions and the branches of knowledge, enlarged by the disciplines, had been so clear and transparent, neither favour nor canvassing would prevail, but if any had arrived at the highest knowledge by the true and sure labours of the doctrines, to them works would be entrusted of their own accord.

beads.greek: quoniam autem ea non sunt inlustria neque apparentia in aspectu, ut putamus oportuisse, et animadverto potius indoctos quam doctos gratia superare, non esse certandum iudicans cum indoctis ambitione, potius his praeceptis editis ostendam nostrae scientiae virtutem.
beads.english: Since, however, these things are not conspicuous nor apparent to sight, as we think they ought to have been, and I observe that the unlearned rather than the learned prevail by favour, judging that one must not contend with the unlearned in canvassing, I shall rather, by publishing these precepts, show the excellence of our knowledge.

beads.greek: [3.pr.4] Itaque, imperator, in primo volumine tibi de arte et quas habeat ea virtutes quibusque disciplinis oporteat esse auctum architectum, exposui et subieci causas, quid ita earum oporteat eum esse peritum, rationesque summae architecturae partitione distribui finitionibusque terminavi.
beads.english: [3.pr.4] Accordingly, Emperor, in the first volume I set out for you concerning the art, and what excellences it has, and with what disciplines the architect ought to be furnished, and I added the reasons why he ought to be skilled in them, and I distributed the principles of the whole of architecture by partition and marked them off with definitions.

beads.greek: deinde, quod erat primum et necessarium, de moenibus, quemadmodum eligantur loci salubres, ratiocinationibus explicui, ventique qui sint et e quibus regionibus singuli spirant, deformationibus grammicis ostendi, platearumque et vicorum uti emendate fiant distributiones in moenibus, docui et ita finitionem primo volumine constitui.
beads.english: Then, as was the first and necessary matter, concerning city walls, I explained with reasoned arguments how healthy sites are to be chosen; and what the winds are and from which quarters each blows, I showed by linear diagrams; and how the allocations of broad streets and lanes within the walls may be made correctly, I taught, and thus I established the conclusion of the first volume.

beads.greek: item in secundo de materia, quas habeat in operibus utilitates et quibus virtutibus e natura rerum est comparata, peregi.
beads.english: Likewise in the second I treated of timber, what uses it has in buildings and with what qualities it is furnished by the nature of things.

beads.greek: nunc in tertio de deorum inmortalium aedibus sacris dicam et, uti oportet, perscriptas exponam.
beads.english: Now in the third I shall speak of the sacred temples of the immortal gods and, as is proper, shall set them forth fully described.

beads.greek: [3.1.1] Aedium compositio constat ex symmetria, cuius rationem diligentissime architecti tenere debent.
beads.english: [3.1.1] The composition of temples consists in symmetry, the principle of which architects must grasp most diligently.

beads.greek: ea autem paritur a proportione, quae graece ἀναλογία dicitur.
beads.english: This, moreover, is begotten from proportion, which in Greek is called ἀναλογία.

beads.greek: proportio est ratae partis membrorum in omni opere totiusque commodulatio, ex qua ratio efficitur symmetriarum.
beads.english: Proportion is the commensuration of a fixed part of the members in every work and of the whole, from which the system of symmetries is produced.

beads.greek: namque non potest aedis ulla sine symmetria atque proportione rationem habere compositionis, nisi uti hominis bene figurati membrorum habuerit exactam rationem.
beads.english: For no temple can have a principle of composition without symmetry and proportion, unless it has an exact system of members, as that of a well-shaped man.

beads.greek: [3.1.2] Corpus enim hominis ita natura composuit, uti os capitis a mento ad frontem summam et radices imas capilli esset decimae partis, item manus pansa ab articulo ad extremum medium digitum tantundem, caput a mento ad summum verticem octavae, cum cervicibus imis ab summo pectore ad imas radices capillorum sextae, a medio pectore ad summum verticem quartae.
beads.english: [3.1.2] For nature has composed the body of a man in such a way that the face of the head, from the chin to the top of the forehead and the lowest roots of the hair, is a tenth part; likewise the open hand, from the wrist-joint to the tip of the middle finger, is just as much; the head from the chin to the top of the crown an eighth; with the lowest part of the neck, from the top of the chest to the lowest roots of the hair, a sixth; from the middle of the chest to the top of the crown a fourth.

beads.greek: ipsius autem oris altitudinis tertia est pars ab imo mento ad imas nares, nasum ab imis naribus ad finem mediûm superciliorum tantundem, ab ea fine ad imas radices capilli frons efficitur item tertiae partis.
beads.english: Of the height of the face itself, a third part is from the bottom of the chin to the bottom of the nostrils; the nose, from the bottom of the nostrils to the boundary between the eyebrows, is just as much; from that boundary to the lowest roots of the hair the forehead is formed, likewise a third part.

beads.greek: pes vero altitudinis corporis sextae, cubitum quartae, pectus item quartae.
beads.english: The foot, indeed, is a sixth of the height of the body, the cubit a fourth, the chest likewise a fourth.

beads.greek: reliqua quoque membra suas habent commensus proportiones, quibus etiam antiqui pictores et statuarii nobiles usi magnas et infinitas laudes sunt adsecuti.
beads.english: The remaining members too have their own proportions of measurement, and by employing these the ancient painters and famous sculptors obtained great and boundless praise.

english_sentences: [3.1.1] The composition of temples consists in symmetry, the principle of which architects must grasp most diligently.
This, moreover, is begotten from proportion, which in Greek is called ἀναλογία.
Proportion is the commensuration of a fixed part of the members in every work and of the whole, from which the system of symmetries is produced.
For no temple can have a principle of composition without symmetry and proportion, unless it has an exact system of members, as that of a well-shaped man.

[3.1.2] For nature has composed the body of a man in such a way that the face of the head, from the chin to the top of the forehead and the lowest roots of the hair, is a tenth part; likewise the open hand, from the wrist-joint to the tip of the middle finger, is just as much; the head from the chin to the top of the crown an eighth; with the lowest part of the neck, from the top of the chest to the lowest roots of the hair, a sixth; from the middle of the chest to the top of the crown a fourth.

Of the height of the face itself, a third part is from the bottom of the chin to the bottom of the nostrils; the nose, from the bottom of the nostrils to the boundary between the eyebrows, is just as much; from that boundary to the lowest roots of the hair the forehead is formed, likewise a third part.
The foot, indeed, is a sixth of the height of the body, the cubit a fourth, the chest likewise a fourth.
The remaining members too have their own proportions of measurement, and by employing these the ancient painters and famous sculptors obtained great and boundless praise.

beads.greek: [3.1.3] Similiter vero sacrarum aedium membra ad universam totius magnitudinis summam ex partibus singulis convenientissimum debent habere commensus responsum.
beads.english: [3.1.3] Similarly, indeed, the members of sacred temples ought to have, from their individual parts, a most fitting correspondence of commensuration to the entire sum of the whole magnitude.

beads.greek: item corporis centrum medium naturaliter est umbilicus.
beads.english: Likewise the central point of the body is naturally the navel.

beads.greek: namque si homo conlocatus fuerit supinus manibus et pedibus pansis circinique conlocatum centrum in umbilico eius, circumagendo rotundationem utrarumque manuum et pedum digiti linea tangentur.
beads.english: For if a man is placed lying on his back with hands and feet spread out, and the centre of a pair of compasses is placed on his navel, then, in describing a circle, the fingers of both hands and the toes of the feet will be touched by the line.

beads.greek: non minus quemadmodum schema rotundationis in corpore efficitur, item quadrata designatio in eo invenietur.
beads.english: No less, just as the figure of a circle is produced in the body, so likewise a square delineation will be found in it.

beads.greek: nam si a pedibus imis ad summum caput mensum erit eaque mensura relata fuerit ad manus pansas, invenietur eadem latitudo uti altitudo, quemadmodum areae, quae ad normam sunt quadratae.
beads.english: For if measurement is taken from the soles of the feet to the top of the head and that measure is referred to the outstretched hands, the breadth will be found to be the same as the height, just as in areas which are squared to the set-square.

beads.greek: [3.1.4] Ergo si ita natura composuit corpus hominis, uti proportionibus membra ad summam figurationem eius respondeant, cum causa constituisse videntur antiqui, ut etiam in operum perfectionibus singulorum membrorum ad universam figurae speciem habeant commensus exactionem.
beads.english: [3.1.4] Therefore, if nature has so composed the body of man that its members answer in their proportions to its total configuration, the ancients seem to have determined with good reason that, in the completions of works also, the individual members should have an exactness of commensuration to the whole appearance of the figure.

beads.greek: igitur cum in omnibus operibus ordines traderent, maxime in aedibus deorum, quod eorum operum et laudes et culpae aeternae solent permanere.
beads.english: Accordingly, while they handed down orders in all works, most of all in the temples of the gods, because both the merits and the faults of these works are wont to remain for ever.

beads.greek: [3.1.5] Nec minus mensurarum rationes, quae in omnibus operibus videntur necessariae esse, ex corporis membris collegerunt, uti digitum, palmum, pedem, cubitum, et eas distribuerunt in perfectum numerum, quem Graeci τέλειον dicunt.
beads.english: [3.1.5] No less did they collect the systems of measures, which seem to be necessary in all works, from the members of the body—such as the digit, the palm, the foot, the cubit—and they distributed these into the perfect number, which the Greeks call τέλειον.

beads.greek: perfectum autem antiqui instituerunt numerum qui decem dicitur; namque ex manibus digitorum numero est inventus.
beads.english: Now the ancients established as perfect the number which is called ten; for it was discovered from the number of the fingers of the hands.

beads.greek: si autem in utrisque palmis ex articulis ab natura decem sunt perfecti, etiam Platoni placuit esse eum numerum ea re perfectum, quod ex X singularibus rebus, quae μονάδες apud Graecos dicuntur, perficitur decusis.
beads.english: And if in both palms ten have been made complete by nature from the joints, it was also Plato's view that this number is perfect for the reason that the decussis (ten) is made complete out of ten single things, which among the Greeks are called μονάδες.

beads.greek: simul autem undecim aut duodecim sunt facti, quod superaverint, non possunt esse perfecti, donec ad alterum decusis perveniant; singulares enim res particulae sunt eius numeri.
beads.english: But as soon as eleven or twelve have been made, because they have gone beyond, they cannot be perfect until they arrive at a second decussis; for the single things are fractional parts of that number.

greek_sentences: [3.1.5] Nec minus mensurarum rationes, quae in omnibus operibus videntur necessariae esse, ex corporis membris collegerunt, uti digitum, palmum, pedem, cubitum, et eas distribuerunt in perfectum numerum, quem Graeci τέλειον dicunt.
perfectum autem antiqui instituerunt numerum qui decem dicitur; namque ex manibus digitorum numero est inventus.

simul autem undecim aut duodecim sunt facti, quod superaverint, non possunt esse perfecti, donec ad alterum decusis perveniant; singulares enim res particulae sunt eius numeri.
english_sentences: [3.1.5] No less did they collect the systems of measures, which seem to be necessary in all works, from the members of the body—such as the digit, the palm, the foot, the cubit—and they distributed these into the perfect number, which the Greeks call τέλειον.
Now the ancients established as perfect the number which is called ten; for it was discovered from the number of the fingers of the hands.

And if in both palms ten have been made complete by nature from the joints, it was also Plato's view that this number is perfect for the reason that the decussis (ten) is made complete out of ten single things, which among the Greeks are called μονάδες.

But as soon as eleven or twelve have been made, because they have gone beyond, they cannot be perfect until they arrive at a second decussis; for the single things are fractional parts of that number.

beads.greek: [3.1.6] Mathematici vero contra disputantes ea re perfectum dixerunt esse numerum qui sex dicitur, quod is numerus habet partitiones eorum rationibus sex numero convenientes sic: sextantem unum, trientes duo, semissem tria, besem quem δίμοιρον dicunt quattuor, quintarium quem πεντάμοιρον dicunt quinque, perfectum sex.
beads.english: [3.1.6] The mathematicians, however, arguing against this, said that the number which is called six is perfect for this reason, that this number has divisions agreeing in their ratios with the number six, thus: a sextans is one, a triens (trientes) two, a semis three, a bes, which they call δίμοιρον, four, a quintarius, which they call πεντάμοιρον, five, the perfect number six.

beads.greek: cum ad duplicationem crescat, supra sex adiecto asse ἔφεκτον ; cum facta sunt octo, quod est tertia adiecta, tertiarium alterum, qui ἐπίτριτος dicitur; dimidia adiecta cum facta sunt novem, sesquialterum, qui ἡμιόλιος appellatur; duabus partibus additis et decusis facto bes alterum, quem ἐπιδίμοιρον vocitant; in undecim numero quod adiecti sunt quinque, quintarium, quem ἐπίπεμπτον dicunt; duodecim autem, quod ex duobus numeris simplicibus est effectus, διπλάσιονα .
beads.english: When it increases towards its doubling: with one as added above six, the ἔφεκτον; when eight has been made, which is a third added, the second tertiarius, which is called ἐπίτριτος; when, with a half added, nine has been made, the sesquialter, which is called ἡμιόλιος; with two parts added and ten made, the second bes, which they call ἐπιδίμοιρον; in the number eleven, because five have been added, the quintarius, which they call ἐπίπεμπτον; twelve, however, because it is produced from two simple numbers, the διπλάσιον.

beads.greek: [3.1.7] Non minus etiam, quod pes hominis altitudinis sextam habet partem, (ita etiam, ex eo quod perficitur pedum numero corporis altitudo, veteribus columnis basis scapi elata sexies altitudines terminavit) eum perfectum constituerunt, cubitumque animadverterunt ex sex palmis constare digitisque XXIIII .
beads.english: [3.1.7] No less also, because the foot of a man has the sixth part of his height (so too, from the fact that the height of the body is completed by the number of feet, in the ancient columns the base of the shaft, raised sixfold, delimited the heights), they established it as perfect, and they observed that the cubit consists of six palms and twenty-four digits.

beads.greek: ex eo etiam videntur civitates Graecorum fecisse, quemadmodum cubitus est sex palmorum, in drachma, qua nummo uterentur, aereos signatos uti asses ex aequo sex, quos obolos appellant, quadrantesque obolorum, quae alii dichalca, nonnulli trichalca dicunt, pro digitis viginti quattuor in drachma constituisse.
beads.english: From this too the cities of the Greeks seem to have done likewise: just as the cubit is of six palms, so in the drachma, which they used as a coin, they seem to have established six stamped bronze pieces, like asses, in equal shares, which they call obols, and the quarter-parts of obols, which some call dichalca and some trichalca, in place of the twenty-four digits in the drachma.

beads.greek: [3.1.8] Nostri autem primo fecerunt perfectum antiquum numerum et in denario denos aeris constituerunt, et ea re compositio nominis ad hodiernum diem denarium retinet.
beads.english: [3.1.8] Our people, however, at first made the ancient number perfect and established in the denarius ten of bronze, and for that reason the composition of the name retains 'denarius' to the present day.

beads.greek: etiamque quarta pars quod efficiebatur ex duobus assibus et tertio semisse, sestertium vocitaverunt.
beads.english: And also the fourth part, because it was made up of two asses and a third half-as, they called the sestertius.

beads.greek: postea autem quam animadverterunt utrosque numeros esse perfectos, et sex et decem, utrosque in unum coiecerunt et fecerunt perfectissimum decusis sexis.
beads.english: But after they observed that both numbers were perfect, both six and ten, they threw both together into one and made the most perfect number, ten-and-six.

beads.greek: huius autem rei auctorem invenerunt pedem.
beads.english: And for this matter they found the foot as their authority.

beads.greek: e cubito enim cum dempti sunt palmi duo, relinquitur pes quattuor palmorum, palmus autem habet quattuor digitos.
beads.english: For when two palms are taken away from the cubit, there remains a foot of four palms, and the palm has four digits.

beads.greek: ita efficitur, ut habeat pes sedecim digitos et totidem asses aeracius denarius.
beads.english: Thus it comes about that the foot has sixteen digits, and the bronze denarius just as many asses.

beads.greek: [3.1.9] Ergo si convenit ex articulis hominis numerum inventum esse et ex membris separatis ad universam corporis speciem ratae partis commensus fieri responsum, relinquitur, ut suspiciamus eos, qui etiam aedes deorum inmortalium constituentes ita membra operum ordinaverunt, ut proportionibus et symmetriis separatae atque universae convenientes efficerentur eorum distributiones.
beads.english: [3.1.9] Therefore, if it is agreed that number was discovered from the joints of the human being, and that from the separate members there arises a correspondence of commensuration of a fixed part to the whole appearance of the body, it remains that we hold in admiration those who, in establishing the temples of the immortal gods as well, so ordered the members of their works that, by proportions and symmetries, their distributions were made to agree both as separate parts and as a whole.

beads.greek: [3.2.1] Aedium autem principia sunt, e quibus constat figurarum aspectus, ea: primum in antis, quod graece ναὸς ἐν παραστάσιν dicitur, deinde prostylos, amphiprostylos, peripteros, pseudodipteros, dipteros , hypaethros.
beads.english: [3.2.1] The principles of temples, from which the appearance of their figures is constituted, are these: first the temple in antis, which in Greek is called naos en parastasin; then the prostyle, the amphiprostyle, the peripteral, the pseudodipteral, the dipteral, the hypaethral.

beads.greek: horum exprimuntur formationes his rationibus.
beads.english: The formations of these are expressed according to the following rules.

beads.greek: [3.2.2] In antis erit aedes, cum habebit in fronte antas parietum, qui cellam circumcludunt, et inter antas in medio columnas duas supraque fastigium symmetria ea conlocatum, quae in hoc libro fuerit perscripta.
beads.english: [3.2.2] A temple will be in antis when it has on the front the antae of the walls which enclose the cella, and between the antae, in the middle, two columns, and above them a pediment placed with that symmetry which shall have been set out in this book.

beads.greek: huius autem exemplar erit ad Tres Fortunas extribus quod est proxime portam Collinam.
beads.english: An example of this will be the one at the Three Fortunes, of the three (extribus) that which is nearest the Colline Gate.

beads.greek: [3.2.3] Prostylos omnia habet quemadmodum in antis, columnas autem contra antas angulares duas supraque epistylia, quemadmodum et in antis, et dextra ac sinistra in versuris singula.
beads.english: [3.2.3] The prostylos has everything in the manner of the in antis, but has two corner columns opposite the antae, and above them epistylia (architraves), just as also in the in antis, and one each on the right and the left at the returns (versurae).

beads.greek: huius exemplar est in insula Tiberina in aede Iovis et Fauni.
beads.english: An example of this is on the Tiber island, in the temple of Jupiter and Faunus.

beads.greek: [3.2.4] amphiprostylos omnia habet ea, quae prostylos, praetereaque habet in postico ad eundem modum columnas et fastigium.
beads.english: [3.2.4] The amphiprostylos has all those things that the prostylos has, and in addition it has, in the rear (posticum), columns and a pediment in the same manner.

beads.greek: [3.2.5] Peripteros autem erit, quae habebit in fronte et postico senas columnas, in lateribus cum angularibus undenas.
beads.english: [3.2.5] The peripteros, however, will be that which will have six columns each at the front and at the rear, and on the flanks eleven each, counting the corner ones.

beads.greek: ita autem sint hae columnae conlocatae, ut intercolumnii latitudinis intervallum sit a parietibus circum ad extremos ordines columnarum, habeatque ambulationem circa cellam aedis, quemadmodum est sine postico in porticu Metelli Iovis Statoris Hermodori et Mariana Honoris et Virtutis a Mucio facta.
beads.english: These columns, moreover, are to be so placed that there is an interval of the width of an intercolumniation from the walls all round to the outermost rows of columns, and that it has a walkway around the cella of the temple, as there is, without a rear (sine postico), in the portico of Metellus in the temple of Jupiter Stator by Hermodorus, and in the Marian temple of Honour and Virtue made by Mucius.

beads.greek: [3.2.6] Pseudodipteros autem sic conlocatur, ut in fronte et postico sint columnae octonae, in lateribus cum angularibus quinae denae.
beads.english: [3.2.6] The pseudodipteros, however, is laid out so that on the front and the rear there are eight columns, and on the flanks, including the corner columns, fifteen.

beads.greek: sint autem parietes cellae contra quaternas columnas medianas in fronte et postico.
beads.english: The walls of the cella, moreover, should stand opposite the four middle columns on the front and the rear.

beads.greek: ita duorum intercolumniorum et imae crassitudinis columnae spatium erit ab parietibus circa ad extremos ordines columnarum.
beads.english: Thus the space from the walls all round to the outermost rows of columns will be that of two intercolumniations plus the thickness of a column at the bottom.

beads.greek: huius exemplar Romae non est, sed Magnesiae Dianae Hermogenis Alabandei et Apollinis a Menesthe facta.
beads.english: There is no example of this at Rome, but at Magnesia there is that of Diana by Hermogenes of Alabanda, and that of Apollo built by Menesthes.

beads.greek: [3.2.7] Dipteros autem octastylos et pronao et postico, sed circa aedem duplices habet ordines columnarum, uti est aedis Quirini dorica et Ephesi Dianae ionica a Chersiphrone constituta.
beads.english: [3.2.7] The dipteros, however, is octastyle both in the pronaos and at the rear, but around the temple it has double rows of columns, as is the Doric temple of Quirinus and the Ionic temple of Diana at Ephesus established by Chersiphron.

beads.greek: [3.2.8] Hypaethros vero decastylos est in pronao et postico.
beads.english: [3.2.8] The hypaethros, in turn, is decastyle in the pronaos and at the rear.

beads.greek: reliqua omnia eadem habet quae dipteros, sed interiore parte columnas in altitudine duplices, remotas a parietibus ad circumitionem ut porticus peristyliorum.
beads.english: In everything else it has the same features as the dipteros, but on the inner side it has columns in two storeys in height, set back from the walls to form a walk-round like the colonnade of peristyles.

beads.greek: medium autem sub divo est sine tecto.
beads.english: The middle, however, is under the open sky, without a roof.

beads.greek: aditus valvarum ex utraque parte in pronao et postico.
beads.english: There are entrances through folding doors on both sides, in the pronaos and at the rear.

beads.greek: huius item exemplar Romae non est, sed Athenis octastylos ex templo Olympio.
beads.english: Of this likewise there is no example at Rome, but at Athens there is the octastyle example from the Olympian temple.

beads.greek: [3.3.1] Species autem aedium sunt quinque, quarum ea sunt vocabula: pycnostylos, id est crebris columnis, systylos paulo remissioribus, diastylos amplius quam oportet inter se diductis, araeostylos spatiis intercolumniorum patentibus rare, eustylos intervallorum iusta distributione.
beads.english: [3.3.1] Now there are five species of temples, of which these are the names: pycnostyle, that is with closely set columns; systyle, with them somewhat more relaxed; diastyle, with them drawn apart from one another more widely than is proper; araeostyle, with the spaces of the intercolumniations standing open thinly; eustyle, with a correct distribution of the intervals.

beads.greek: [3.3.2] Ergo pycnostylos est, cuius intercolumnio unius et dimidiatae columnae crassitudo interponi potest, quemadmodum est divi Iulii et in Caesaris foro Veneris et si quae aliae sic sunt compositae.
beads.english: [3.3.2] Accordingly the pycnostyle is that in whose intercolumniation the thickness of one and a half columns can be inserted, as is the temple of the deified Julius and that of Venus in the forum of Caesar, and any others that are composed in this way.

beads.greek: item systylos est, in qua duarum columnarum crassitudo in intercolumnio poterit conlocari, et spirarum plinthides aeque magnae sint ei spatio, quod fuerit inter duas plinthides, quemadmodum est Fortunae Equestris ad theatrum lapideum reliquaeque, quae eisdem rationibus sunt compositae.
beads.english: Likewise the systyle is that in which the thickness of two columns can be placed in the intercolumniation, and the plinths of the bases are equal in size to the space which there shall be between two plinths, as is the temple of Fortuna Equestris near the stone theatre and the rest which are composed according to the same principles.

greek_sentences: [3.3.1] Species autem aedium sunt quinque, quarum ea sunt vocabula: pycnostylos, id est crebris columnis, systylos paulo remissioribus, diastylos amplius quam oportet inter se diductis, araeostylos spatiis intercolumniorum patentibus rare, eustylos intervallorum iusta distributione.

[3.3.2] Ergo pycnostylos est, cuius intercolumnio unius et dimidiatae columnae crassitudo interponi potest, quemadmodum est divi Iulii et in Caesaris foro Veneris et si quae aliae sic sunt compositae.

english_sentences: [3.3.1] Now there are five species of temples, of which these are the names: pycnostyle, that is with closely set columns; systyle, with them somewhat more relaxed; diastyle, with them drawn apart from one another more widely than is proper; araeostyle, with the spaces of the intercolumniations standing open thinly; eustyle, with a correct distribution of the intervals.

[3.3.2] Accordingly the pycnostyle is that in whose intercolumniation the thickness of one and a half columns can be inserted, as is the temple of the deified Julius and that of Venus in the forum of Caesar, and any others that are composed in this way.

Likewise the systyle is that in which the thickness of two columns can be placed in the intercolumniation, and the plinths of the bases are equal in size to the space which there shall be between two plinths, as is the temple of Fortuna Equestris near the stone theatre and the rest which are composed according to the same principles.

beads.greek: [3.3.3] Haec utraque genera vitiosum habent usum.
beads.english: [3.3.3] Both these kinds have a faulty use.

beads.greek: matres enim familiarum cum ad supplicationem gradibus ascendunt, non possunt per intercolumnia amplexae adire, nisi ordines fecerint; item valvarum aspectus abstruditur columnarum crebritate ipsaque signa obscurantur; item circa aedem propter angustias inpediuntur ambulationes.
beads.english: For mothers of families, when they ascend the steps for a supplication, cannot approach through the intercolumniations arm-in-arm, unless they form single files; likewise the view of the folding doors is shut off by the crowding of the columns, and the statues themselves are obscured; likewise the walks around the temple are impeded on account of the narrowness.

beads.greek: [3.3.4] Diastyli autem haec erit compositio, cum trium columnarum crassitudinem intercolumnio interponere possumus, tamquam est Apollinis et Dianae aedis.
beads.english: [3.3.4] The composition of the diastyle, however, will be this: when we can place the thickness of three columns in the intercolumniation, as is the temple of Apollo and Diana.

beads.greek: haec dispositio hanc habet difficultatem, quod epistylia propter intervallorum magnitudinem franguntur.
beads.english: This arrangement has this difficulty, that the epistyles are broken on account of the size of the intervals.

beads.greek: [3.3.5] In araeostylis autem nec lapideis nec marmoreis epistyliis uti datur, sed inponendae de materia trabes perpetuae.
beads.english: [3.3.5] In araeostyles, however, it is not granted to use epistyles either of stone or of marble, but continuous beams of timber must be laid on.

beads.greek: et ipsarum aedium species sunt varicae, barycephalae, humiles, latae, ornanturque signis fictilibus aut aereis inauratis earum fastigia tuscanico more, uti est ad Circum Maximum Cereris et Herculis Pompeiani, item Capitolii.
beads.english: And the appearances of the temples themselves are splay-legged, heavy-headed, low, broad, and their pediments are adorned with statues of terracotta or of gilded bronze in the Tuscan manner, as is that of Ceres near the Circus Maximus and of Hercules Pompeianus, likewise of the Capitol.

beads.greek: [3.3.6] Reddenda nunc est eustyli ratio, quae maxime probabilis et ad usum et ad speciem et ad firmitatem rationes habet explicatas.
beads.english: [3.3.6] Now the system of the eustyle must be set forth, which is most to be approved and has its principles worked out with regard to use, to appearance and to firmness.

beads.greek: namque facienda sunt in intervallis spatia duarum columnarum et quartae partis columnae crassitudinis, mediumque intercolumnium unum, quod erit in fronte, alterum, quod in postico, trium columnarum crassitudine.
beads.english: For in the intervals spaces of two columns and a quarter part of a column's thickness are to be made, and the middle intercolumniation, the one which will be on the front and the other which is on the rear, of three columns' thickness.

beads.greek: sic enim habebit et figurationis aspectum venustum et aditus usum sine inpeditionibus et circa cellam ambulatio auctoritatem.
beads.english: For thus it will have both a pleasing appearance in its configuration and the use of the approach without impediments, and the walk around the cella will have dignity.

beads.greek: [3.3.7] Huius autem rei ratio explicabitur sic.
beads.english: [3.3.7] The system of this matter will be explained thus.

beads.greek: frons loci quae in aede constituta fuerit, si tetrastylos facienda fuerit, dividatur in partes XI S praeter crepidines et proiecturas spirarum; si sex erit columnarum, in partes XVIII ; si octastylos constituetur, dividatur in XXIV et semissem.
beads.english: The front of the site which shall have been established for the temple, if it is to be made tetrastyle, let it be divided into eleven and a half parts, excluding the crepidines (stepped platform) and the projections of the bases (spirae); if it will be of six columns, into eighteen parts; if it is to be set up octastyle, let it be divided into twenty-four and a half.

beads.greek: item ex his partibus sive tetrastyli sive hexastyli sive octastyli una pars sumatur, eaque erit modulus.
beads.english: Likewise from these parts, whether of the tetrastyle, of the hexastyle, or of the octastyle, let one part be taken, and that will be the module.

beads.greek: cuius moduli unus erit crassitudinis columnarum.
beads.english: Of this module one will be the thickness of the columns.

beads.greek: intercolumnia singula, praeter media, modulorum duorum et moduli quartae partis; mediana in fronte et postico singula ternûm modulorum.
beads.english: The single intercolumniations, except the middle ones, of two modules and a quarter part of a module; the middle ones on the front and on the rear of three modules each.

beads.greek: ipsarum columnarum altitudo modulorum VIIII et dimidiae moduli partis.
beads.english: The height of the columns themselves of nine modules and a half part of a module.

beads.greek: ita ex ea divisione intercolumnia altitudinesque columnarum habebunt iustam rationem.
beads.english: Thus from this division the intercolumniations and the heights of the columns will have a correct proportion.

beads.greek: [3.3.8] Huius exemplar Romae nullum habemus, sed in Asia Teo hexastylon Liberi Patris.
beads.english: [3.3.8] Of this we have no example at Rome, but in Asia, at Teos, there is the hexastyle temple of Liber Pater.

beads.greek: Eas autem symmetrias constituit Hermogenes, qui etiam primus invenit octastylon pseudodipterive rationem.
beads.english: These symmetries, moreover, were established by Hermogenes, who was also the first to devise the octastyle, or the system of the pseudodipteros.

beads.greek: ex dipteri enim aedis symmetria distulit interiores ordines columnarum XXXIV eaque ratione sumptus operasque compendii fecit.
beads.english: For from the symmetry of the dipteral temple he removed the inner rows of columns, thirty-four in number, and by that method made a saving of expense and labour.

beads.greek: is in medio ambulationi laxamentum egregie circa cellam fecit de aspectuque nihil inminuit, sed sine desiderio supervacuorum conservavit auctoritatem totius operis distributione.
beads.english: He admirably created in the middle an open space for walking around the cella, and he took nothing away from the appearance, but, without any sense of want of the superfluous parts, preserved the authority of the whole work by his distribution.

beads.greek: [3.3.9] Pteromatos enim ratio et columnarum circum aedem dispositio ideo est inventa, ut aspectus propter asperitatem intercolumniorum habeat auctoritatem, praeterea, si ex improviso imbrium aquae vis occupaverit et intercluserit hominum multitudinem, ut habeat in aede circaque cellam cum laxamento liberam moram.
beads.english: [3.3.9] For the system of the pteroma and the disposition of columns around the temple was devised for this reason: that the view might have authority on account of the roughness of the intercolumniations, and further, that if the violence of rain-water should unexpectedly overtake and cut off a crowd of people, it might have in the temple and around the cella a free place to wait, with room to spare.

beads.greek: haec autem ut explicantur in pseudodipteris aedium dispositionibus!
beads.english: And these things, how they are set out in the pseudodipteral arrangements of temples!

beads.greek: quare videtur acuta magnaque sollertia effectus operum Hermogenes fecisse reliquisseque fontes, unde posteri possent haurire disciplinarum rationes.
beads.english: Wherefore Hermogenes seems with keen and great ingenuity to have produced the effects of his works, and to have left springs from which posterity could draw the principles of the disciplines.

english_sentences: [3.3.8] Of this we have no example at Rome, but in Asia, at Teos, there is the hexastyle temple of Liber Pater.
These symmetries, moreover, were established by Hermogenes, who was also the first to devise the octastyle, or the system of the pseudodipteros.
For from the symmetry of the dipteral temple he removed the inner rows of columns, thirty-four in number, and by that method made a saving of expense and labour.

He admirably created in the middle an open space for walking around the cella, and he took nothing away from the appearance, but, without any sense of want of the superfluous parts, preserved the authority of the whole work by his distribution.

[3.3.9] For the system of the pteroma and the disposition of columns around the temple was devised for this reason: that the view might have authority on account of the roughness of the intercolumniations, and further, that if the violence of rain-water should unexpectedly overtake and cut off a crowd of people, it might have in the temple and around the cella a free place to wait, with room to spare.
And these things, how they are set out in the pseudodipteral arrangements of temples!
Wherefore Hermogenes seems with keen and great ingenuity to have produced the effects of his works, and to have left springs from which posterity could draw the principles of the disciplines.

beads.greek: [3.3.10] Aedibus araeostylis columnae sic sunt faciendae, uti crassitudines earum sint partis octavae ad altitudines.
beads.english: [3.3.10] In araeostyle temples the columns are to be made so that their thicknesses are an eighth part of their heights.

beads.greek: item in diastylo dimetienda est altitudo columnae in partes octo et dimidiam, et unius partis columnae crassitudo conlocetur.
beads.english: Likewise in the diastyle the height of the column is to be measured out into eight and a half parts, and the thickness of the column is to be set at one part.

beads.greek: in systylo altitudo dividatur in novem et dimidiam partem, et ex eis una ad crassitudinem columnae detur.
beads.english: In the systyle let the height be divided into nine and a half parts, and of these let one be given to the thickness of the column.

beads.greek: item in pycnostylo dividenda est altitudo in partes decem, et eius una pars facienda est columnae crassitudo.
beads.english: Likewise in the pycnostyle the height is to be divided into ten parts, and one part of it is to be made the thickness of the column.

beads.greek: eustyli autem aedis columnae, uti systyli, in novem partes altitudo dividatur et dimidiam partem, et eius una pars constituatur in crassitudine imi scapi.
beads.english: But as for the columns of a eustyle temple, as in the systyle, let the height be divided into nine parts and a half part, and let one part of it be established as the thickness of the lower shaft.

beads.greek: ita habebitur pro rata parte intercolumniorum ratio.
beads.english: Thus the ratio of the intercolumniations will be obtained in due proportion.

beads.greek: [3.3.11] Quemadmodum enim crescunt spatia inter columnas, proportionibus adaugendae sunt crassitudines scaporum.
beads.english: [3.3.11] For as the spaces between the columns increase, the thicknesses of the shafts must be augmented in proportion.

beads.greek: namque si in araeostylo nona aut decima pars crassitudinis fuerit, tenuis et exilis apparebit, ideo quod per latitudinem intercolumniorum aer consumit et inminuit aspectu scaporum crassitudinem.
beads.english: For if in the araeostyle the thickness were a ninth or a tenth part, it will appear thin and meagre, because through the width of the intercolumniations the air consumes and diminishes to the eye the thickness of the shafts.

beads.greek: contra vero pycnostylis si octava pars crassitudinis fuerit, propter crebritatem et angustias intercolumniorum tumidam et invenustam efficiet speciem.
beads.english: Conversely, in pycnostyles, if the thickness were an eighth part, on account of the closeness and narrowness of the intercolumniations it will produce a swollen and ungraceful appearance.

beads.greek: itaque generis operis oportet persequi symmetrias.
beads.english: Therefore one must follow the symmetries of each kind of work.

beads.greek: etiamque angulares columnae crassiores faciendae sunt ex sua diametro quinquagesima parte, quod eae ab aere circumciduntur et graciliores videntur esse aspicientibus.
beads.english: And also the corner columns are to be made thicker by a fiftieth part of their own diameter, because they are cut around by the air and seem to those viewing them to be more slender.

beads.greek: ergo quod oculus fallit, ratiocinatione est exaequandum.
beads.english: Therefore what deceives the eye must be compensated by calculation.

english_sentences: [3.3.10] In araeostyle temples the columns are to be made so that their thicknesses are an eighth part of their heights.
Likewise in the diastyle the height of the column is to be measured out into eight and a half parts, and the thickness of the column is to be set at one part.
In the systyle let the height be divided into nine and a half parts, and of these let one be given to the thickness of the column.
Likewise in the pycnostyle the height is to be divided into ten parts, and one part of it is to be made the thickness of the column.
But as for the columns of a eustyle temple, as in the systyle, let the height be divided into nine parts and a half part, and let one part of it be established as the thickness of the lower shaft.
Thus the ratio of the intercolumniations will be obtained in due proportion.
[3.3.11] For as the spaces between the columns increase, the thicknesses of the shafts must be augmented in proportion.

For if in the araeostyle the thickness were a ninth or a tenth part, it will appear thin and meagre, because through the width of the intercolumniations the air consumes and diminishes to the eye the thickness of the shafts.
Conversely, in pycnostyles, if the thickness were an eighth part, on account of the closeness and narrowness of the intercolumniations it will produce a swollen and ungraceful appearance.
Therefore one must follow the symmetries of each kind of work.
And also the corner columns are to be made thicker by a fiftieth part of their own diameter, because they are cut around by the air and seem to those viewing them to be more slender.
Therefore what deceives the eye must be compensated by calculation.

beads.greek: [3.3.12] Contracturae autem in summis columnarum hypotracheliis ita faciendae videntur, uti, si columna sit ab minimo ad pedes quinos denos, ima crassitudo dividatur in partes sex et earum partium quinque summa constituatur.
beads.english: [3.3.12] The contractions, moreover, at the uppermost hypotrachelia of the columns seem to be made as follows: if a column is from the smallest size up to fifteen feet, let the lowest thickness be divided into six parts, and let the top be fixed at five of those parts.

beads.greek: item quae erit ab quindecim pedibus ad pedes viginti, scapus imus in partes sex et semissem dividatur, earumque partium quinque et semisse superior crassitudo columnae fiat.
beads.english: Likewise, one that will be from fifteen feet to twenty feet, let the lowest shaft be divided into six parts and a half, and let the upper thickness of the column be made of five and a half of those parts.

beads.greek: item quae erunt a pedibus viginti ad pedes triginta, scapus imus dividatur in partes septem, earumque sex summa contractura perficiatur.
beads.english: Likewise, those that will be from twenty feet to thirty feet, let the lowest shaft be divided into seven parts, and let the contraction at the top be completed at six of them.

beads.greek: quae autem ab triginta pedibus ad quadraginta alta erit, ima dividatur in partes septem et dimidiam; ex his sex et dimidiam in summo habeat contracturae rationem.
beads.english: But one that will be from thirty feet to forty in height, let the bottom be divided into seven parts and a half; of these let it have six and a half at the top as the measure of the contraction.

beads.greek: quae erunt ab quadraginta pedibus ad quinquaginta, item dividendae sunt in octo partes, et earum septem in summo scapo sub capitulo contrahantur.
beads.english: Those that will be from forty feet to fifty, likewise, are to be divided into eight parts, and let them be contracted to seven of these at the top of the shaft beneath the capital.

beads.greek: item si quae altiores erunt, eadem ratione pro rata constituantur contracturae.
beads.english: Likewise, if any will be taller, let the contractions be fixed in the same manner in due proportion.

Likewise, if any will be taller, let the contractions be fixed in the same manner in due proportion.

beads.greek: [3.3.13] Haec autem propter altitudinis intervallum scandentis oculi species adiciuntur crassitudinibus temperaturae.
beads.english: [3.3.13] These additions, however, are made to the thicknesses, by way of tempering, on account of the interval of height through which the sight of the eye climbs.

beads.greek: venustates enim persequitur visus, cuius si non blandimur voluptati proportione et modulorum adiectionibus, uti quod fallitur temperatione adaugeatur, vastus et invenustus conspicientibus remittetur aspectus.
beads.english: For the sight pursues graces, and if we do not flatter its pleasure by proportion and by additions of modules, so that what is deceived may be augmented by tempering, an ungainly and graceless appearance will be sent back to those who look on.

beads.greek: de adiectione, quae adicitur in mediis columnis, quae apud Graecos ἔντασις appellatur, in extremo libro erit forma et ratio eius, quemadmodum mollis et conveniens efficiatur, subscripta.
beads.english: Concerning the addition which is added at the middle of columns, which among the Greeks is called ἔντασις, its figure and method, how it is made soft and suitable, will be set down at the end of the book.

beads.greek: [3.4.1] Fundationes eorum operum fodiantur, si queat inveniri, ad solidum et in solido, quantum ex amplitudine operis pro ratione videbitur, extruaturque structura totum solum quam solidissima.
beads.english: [3.4.1] Let the foundations of those works be dug, if it can be found, down to solid ground and into solid ground, as much as will seem fitting in proportion to the size of the work, and let the whole bottom be built up with masonry as solid as possible.

beads.greek: supraque terram parietes extruantur sub columnas dimidio crassiores quam columnae sunt futurae, uti firmiora sint inferiora superioribus; quae stereobates appellantur, nam excipiunt onera.
beads.english: And above the ground let walls be built beneath the columns, thicker by a half than the columns are going to be, so that the lower parts may be firmer than the upper; these are called stereobates, for they receive the loads.

beads.greek: spirarumque proiecturae non procedant extra solidum; item supra parietis ad eundem modum crassitudo servanda est.
beads.english: And let the projections of the bases not advance beyond the solid; likewise the thickness of the wall above is to be kept to the same measure.

beads.greek: intervalla autem concamaranda aut solidanda festucationibus, uti distineantur.
beads.english: The intervals, moreover, are to be vaulted over or made solid with rammed fillings (festucationibus), so that they are held apart.

beads.greek: [3.4.2] Sin autem solidum non invenietur, sed locus erit congesticius ad imum aut paluster, tunc is locus fodiatur exinaniaturque et palis alneis aut oleagineis aut robusteis ustilatis configatur, sublicaque machinis adigatur quam creberrime, carbonibusque expleantur intervalla palorum, et tunc structuris solidissimis fundamenta impleantur.
beads.english: [3.4.2] But if solid ground is not found, and the place is made-up soil down to the bottom, or marshy, then that place is to be dug out and emptied, and driven full of piles of alder or of olive or of oak, charred, and the piling is to be driven down by machines as closely as possible, and the intervals between the piles are to be filled up with charcoal, and then the foundations are to be filled in with the most solid masonry.

beads.greek: extructis autem fundamentis ad libramentum stylobatae sunt conlocandi.
beads.english: When the foundations have been built up, the stylobates are to be set in place to the level.

beads.greek: [3.4.3] Supra stylobatas columnae disponendae, quemadmodum supra scriptum est, sive in pycnostylo, quemadmodum pycnostyla, sive systylo aut diastylo aut eustylo, quemadmodum supra scripta sunt et constituta.
beads.english: [3.4.3] Upon the stylobates the columns are to be arranged, as has been written above, whether in the pycnostyle, as pycnostyle temples are, or in the systyle or diastyle or eustyle, as these have been described and laid down above.

beads.greek: in araeostylis enim libertas est quantum cuique libet constituendi.
beads.english: For in araeostyle temples there is freedom to lay them out as each person pleases.

beads.greek: sed ita columnae in peripteris conlocentur, uti, quot intercolumnia sunt in fronte, totidem bis intercolumnia fiant in lateribus; ita enim erit duplex longitudo operis ad latitudinem.
beads.english: But the columns in peripteral temples are to be set so that, however many intercolumniations there are in the front, twice as many intercolumniations are made on the flanks; for thus the length of the work will be double its width.

beads.greek: namque qui columnarum duplicationes fecerunt, erravisse videntur, quod unum intercolumnium in longitudine plus quam oporteat procurrere videtur.
beads.english: For those who have made the doublings of the columns appear to have erred, because one intercolumniation seems to run out in the length more than it ought.

beads.greek: [3.4.4] Gradus in fronte constituendi ita sunt, uti sint semper inpares; namque cum dextro pede primus gradus ascendatur, item in summo templo primus erit ponendus.
beads.english: [3.4.4] The steps at the front are to be so arranged that they are always odd in number; for since the first step is mounted with the right foot, the right foot will likewise be the first to be set down at the top of the temple.

beads.greek: crassitudines autem eorum graduum ita finiendas censeo, ut neque crassiores dextante nec tenuiores dodrante sint conlocatae; sic enim durus non erit ascensus.
beads.english: The thicknesses (risers) of these steps I think should be so limited that they are placed neither thicker than ten twelfths of a foot (a dextans) nor thinner than nine twelfths (a dodrans); for thus the ascent will not be hard.

beads.greek: retractiones autem graduum nec minus quam sesquipedales nec plus quam bipedales faciendae videntur.
beads.english: The treads (retractiones) of the steps, it seems, should be made neither less than a foot and a half nor more than two feet.

beads.greek: item si circa aedem gradus futuri sunt, ad eundem modum fieri debent.
beads.english: Likewise, if there are to be steps around the temple, they ought to be made in the same manner.

beads.greek: [3.4.5] Sin autem circa aedem ex tribus lateribus podium faciendum erit, id constituatur, uti quadrae, spirae, trunci, coronae, lysis ad ipsum stylobatam, qui erit sub columnarum spiris, conveniant.
beads.english: [3.4.5] But if a podium is to be made around the temple on three sides, it should be so constructed that its plinths (quadrae), bases (spirae), dadoes (trunci), cornices (coronae) and lysis agree with the stylobate itself, which will be beneath the bases of the columns.

beads.greek: stylobatam ita oportet exaequari, uti habeat per medium adiectionem per scamillos inpares; si enim ad libellam dirigetur, alveolatum oculo videbitur.
beads.english: The stylobate ought to be so levelled that it has an addition (adiectio) through the middle by means of unequal scamilli (scamillos inpares); for if it is set out to the level (libella), it will appear to the eye hollowed like a channel (alveolatum).

beads.greek: hoc autem, ut scamilli ad id convenientes fiant, item in extremo libro forma et demonstratio erit descripta.
beads.english: As to this, how the scamilli are to be made suitable for that purpose, a figure and demonstration will likewise be drawn out at the end of the book.

beads.greek: [3.5.1] His perfectis in suis locis spirae conlocentur, eaeque ad symmetriam sic perficiantur, uti crassitudo cum plintho sit columnae ex dimidia crassitudine proiecturamque, quam Graeci ἐκφοράν vocitant, habeant S extantem: ita tum lata et longa erit columnae crassitudinis unius et dimidiae.
beads.english: [3.5.1] When these things have been completed, let the bases (spirae) be set in their places, and let them be finished to a symmetry such that the thickness together with the plinth is of half the thickness of the column, and that they have a projection, which the Greeks call ἐκφορά, standing out by a half (S): thus it will then be one and a half column-thicknesses wide and long.

beads.greek: [3.5.2] Altitudo eius, si atticurges erit, ita dividatur, ut superior pars tertia parte sit crassitudinis columnae, reliquum plintho relinquatur.
beads.english: [3.5.2] Its height, if it is to be Attic (atticurges), is to be divided in such a way that the upper part is one third of the thickness of the column, and the remainder is left for the plinth.

beads.greek: dempta plintho reliquum dividatur in partes quattuor, fiatque superior torus quartae; reliquae tres aequaliter dividantur, et una sit inferior torus, altera pars cum suis quadris scotia, quam Graeci τροχίλον dicunt.
beads.english: With the plinth removed, let the remainder be divided into four parts, and let the upper torus be made of one quarter; let the remaining three be divided equally, and let one be the lower torus, the other part, together with its fillets (quadrae), the scotia, which the Greeks call τροχίλος.

beads.greek: [3.5.3] Sin autem ionicae erunt faciendae, symmetriae earum sic erunt constituendae, uti latitudo spirae quoqueversus sit columnae crassitudinis adiecta e crassitudine quarta et octava.
beads.english: [3.5.3] But if they are to be made Ionic, their symmetries are to be established in such a way that the width of the base in every direction is the thickness of the column with a quarter and an eighth of the thickness added.

beads.greek: altitudo ita uti atticurges; item et eius plinthos; reliquumque praeter plinthum, quod erit tertia pars crassitudinis columnae, dividatur in partes septem: inde trium partium torus, qui est in summo; reliquae quattuor partes dividendae sunt aequaliter, et una pars fiat cum suis astragalis et supercilio superior trochilus, altera pars inferiori trochilo relinquatur; sed inferior maior apparebit, ideo quod habebit ad extremam plinthum proiecturam.
beads.english: The height as for the Attic; likewise also its plinth; and the remainder, apart from the plinth, which will be a third part of the thickness of the column, is to be divided into seven parts: of these, the torus which is at the top is of three parts; the remaining four parts are to be divided equally, and let one part, with its astragals and its supercilium, be made the upper trochilus, and let the other part be left for the lower trochilus; but the lower will appear larger, because it will have a projection out to the edge of the plinth.

beads.greek: astragali faciendi sunt octavae partis trochili.
beads.english: The astragals are to be made of an eighth part of the trochilus.

beads.greek: proiectura erit spirae pars octava et sexta decuma pars crassitudinis columnae.
beads.english: The projection of the base will be an eighth part and a sixteenth part of the thickness of the column.

beads.greek: [3.5.4] Spiris perfectis et conlocatis columnae sunt medianae in pronao et postico ad perpendiculum medii centri conlocandae, angulares autem quaeque e regione earum futurae sunt in lateribus aedis dextra ac sinistra, uti partes interiores, quae ad parietes cellae spectant, ad perpendiculum latus habeant conlocatum, exteriores autem partes †uti dicant se earum contracturam.

beads.greek: sic enim erunt figurae compositionis aedium contractura eius tali ratione exactae.
beads.english: For in this way the figures of the composition of temples will have been worked out exactly, with its contraction, by such a method.

beads.greek: [3.5.5] Scapis columnarum statutis capitulorum ratio sic est habenda.
beads.english: [3.5.5] When the shafts of the columns have been set up, the system of the capitals is to be handled as follows.

beads.greek: si pulvinata erunt, his symmetriis conformabuntur, uti, quam crassus imus scapus fuerit addita octava decuma parte scapi, abacus habeat longitudinem et latitudinem; crassitudinem cum volutis eius dimidiam.
beads.english: If they are to be cushion-shaped, they shall be formed according to these symmetries: that the abacus shall have as its length and breadth the thickness of the lowest part of the shaft with an eighteenth part of the shaft added; its thickness, together with the volutes, half of that.

beads.greek: recedendum autem est ab extremo abaco in interiorem partem frontibus volutarum parte duodevicensima et eius dimidia.
beads.english: One must recede, moreover, from the edge of the abacus toward the inner part, for the fronts of the volutes, by an eighteenth part and a half of it.

beads.greek: tunc crassitudo dividenda est in partes novem et dimidiam, et secundum abacum in quattuor partibus volutarum secundum extremi abaci quadram lineae demittendae, quae cathetoe dicuntur.
beads.english: Then the thickness is to be divided into nine and a half parts, and along the abacus, at the four parts of the volutes, lines are to be let down following the squared edge of the outermost abacus, which are called cathetoe.

beads.greek: tunc ex novem partibus et dimidia una pars et dimidia abaci crassitudo relinquatur, reliquae octo volutis constituantur.
beads.english: Then of the nine and a half parts one part and a half is to be left for the thickness of the abacus; the remaining eight are to be assigned to the volutes.

beads.english: Next let these lines be divided in such a way that four and a half parts are left beneath the abacus.

beads.greek: tunc in eo loco, qui locus dividit quattuor et dimidiam et tres et dimidiam partem, centrum oculi conlocetur signeturque ex eo centro rotunda circinatio tam magna in diametro, quam una pars ex octo partibus est.
beads.english: Then at that place, the place which divides the four and a half and the three and a half parts, let the centre of the eye be placed, and from that centre let a round circle be marked out as great in diameter as one part out of the eight parts is.

beads.greek: ea erit oculi magnitudine, et in ea catheto respondens diametros agatur.
beads.english: That will be the size of the eye, and in it let a diameter be drawn corresponding to the cathetus.

beads.greek: tunc ab summo sub abaco inceptum schema volutae in singulis tetrantorum actionibus dimidiatum oculi spatium minuatur, doneque in eundem tetrantem, qui subest, conveniat.
beads.english: Then, beginning from the top beneath the abacus, let the outline of the volute be diminished, in each of the sweeps of the quadrants, by half the space of the eye, until it comes together into the same quadrant which lies beneath.

beads.greek: [3.5.7] Capituli autem crassitudo sic est facienda, ut ex novem partibus et dimidia tres partes praependeant infra astragalum summi scapi; cymatio, adempto abaco et canali, reliqua sit pars.
beads.english: [3.5.7] The thickness of the capital, however, is to be made in such a way that, of nine and a half parts, three parts hang down below the astragal of the top of the shaft; to the cymatium, once the abacus and the channel have been taken away, let the remaining part belong.

beads.greek: proiectura autem cymatii habeat extra abaci quadram oculi magnitudinem.
beads.english: The projection of the cymatium, moreover, should have, beyond the square of the abacus, the magnitude of the eye.

beads.greek: pulvinorum baltei ab abaco hanc habeant proiecturam, uti circini centrum unum cum sit positum in capituli tetrante et alterum diducatur ad extremum cymatium, circumactum balteorum extremas partes tangat.
beads.english: The belts of the bolsters should have this projection from the abacus: that when one point of the compasses is set in the tetrans (quadrant) of the capital and the other is drawn out to the outermost edge of the cymatium, the circle thus swept round (circumactum) touches the outermost parts of the belts.

beads.greek: axes volutarum ne crassiores sint quam oculi magnitudo, volutaeque ipsae succidantur altitudinis suae duodecimam partem.
beads.english: The axes of the volutes should not be thicker than the magnitude of the eye, and the volutes themselves should be cut back by a twelfth part of their height.

beads.greek: haec erunt symmetriae capitulorum, quae columnae futurae sunt ab minimo ad pedes XXV .
beads.english: These will be the symmetries of capitals for columns that are to be from the smallest up to 25 feet.

beads.greek: quae supra erunt, reliqua habebunt ad eundem modum symmetrias, abacus autem erit longus et latus, quam crassa columna est ima adiecta parte VIIII , uti, quo minus habuerit altior columna contractum, eo ne minus habeat capitulum suae symmetriae proiecturam et in latitudine suae partis adiectionem.
beads.english: Those which are above that will have the remaining symmetries in the same manner, but the abacus will be as long and as wide as the column is thick at the bottom with a ninth part added, so that, in proportion as the taller column has less contraction, the capital shall not have less projection of its symmetry, nor less addition of its part in width.

beads.greek: [3.5.8] De volutarum descriptionibus, uti ad circinum sint recte involutae, quemadmodum describantur, in extremo libro forma et ratio earum erit subscripta.
beads.english: [3.5.8] As to the drawing of the volutes, so that they may be correctly wound with the compasses, in what manner they are to be drawn, their figure and method will be set down at the end of the book.

beads.greek: Capitulis perfectis, deinde in scapis columnarum non ad libellam sed ad aequalem modulum conlocatis, ut, quae adiectio in stylobatis facta fuerit, in superioribus membris respondeat , epistyliorum ratio sic est habenda, uti, si columnae fuerint a minima XII pedum ad quindecim pedes, epistylii sit altitudo dimidia crassitudinis imae columnae; item si ab XV pedibus ad XX , columnae altitudo dimetiatur in partes tredecim, et unius partis altitudo epistylii fiat; item si XX ad XXV pedes, dividatur altitudo in partes XII et semissem, et eius una pars epistylium in altitudine fiat; item si ab XXV pedibus ad XXX , dividatur in partes XII , et eius una pars altitudo fiat.
beads.english: When the capitals have been finished, and then set upon the shafts of the columns, not to a level but to an equal module, so that the addition which has been made in the stylobates may correspond in the upper members, the proportion of the epistyles is to be reckoned thus: if the columns are from the smallest, of 12 feet, up to fifteen feet, let the height of the epistyle be half the thickness of the bottom of the column; likewise if from 15 feet to 20, let the height of the column be measured out into thirteen parts, and let the height of the epistyle be made one part; likewise if from 20 to 25 feet, let the height be divided into 12 parts and a half, and let the epistyle be made one part of it in height; likewise if from 25 feet to 30, let it be divided into 12 parts, and let the height be made one part of it.

beads.greek: item si quae altiores erunt, rata parte ad eundem modum ex altitudine columnarum expediendae sunt altitudines epistyliorum.
beads.english: Likewise if any are taller, the heights of the epistyles are to be worked out in proportion, in the same manner, from the height of the columns.

beads.greek: [3.5.9] Quo altius enim scandit oculi species, non facile persecat aeris crebritatem; dilapsa itaque altitudinis spatio et viribus exuta incertam modulorum renuntiat sensibus quantitatem.
beads.english: [3.5.9] For the higher the sight of the eye climbs, the less easily does it cut through the density of the air; and so, dissipated by the extent of the height and stripped of its strength, it reports to the senses an uncertain quantity of the modules.

beads.greek: quare semper adiciendum est rationis supplementum in symmetriarum membris, ut, cum fuerint aut altioribus locis opera aut etiam ipsa colossicotera, habeant magnitudinum rationem.
beads.english: Wherefore a supplement of proportion must always be added in the members of the symmetries, so that, when works are either in higher places or even themselves more colossal, they may have a proportion of their magnitudes.

beads.greek: epistylii latitudo in imo, quod supra capitulum erit, quanta crassitudo summae columnae sub capitulo erit, tanta fiat; summum, quantum imus scapus.
beads.english: The width of the epistyle at the bottom, which will be above the capital, should be made as great as the thickness of the top of the column beneath the capital will be; the top, as great as the bottom of the shaft.

beads.greek: [3.5.10] Cymatium epistylii septima parte suae altitudinis est faciendum, et in proiectura tantundem.
beads.english: [3.5.10] The cymatium of the epistyle is to be made one seventh part of its height, and in projection the same amount.

beads.greek: reliqua pars praeter cymatium dividenda est in partes XII , et earum trium ima fascia est facienda, secunda IIII , summa V .
beads.english: The remaining part, apart from the cymatium, is to be divided into twelve parts, and of these the lowest fascia is to be made of three, the second of four, the topmost of five.

beads.greek: item zophorus supra epistylium quarta parte minus altus quam epistylium; sin autem sigilla designari oportuerit, quarta parte altior quam epistylium, uti auctoritatem habeant scalpturae.
beads.english: Likewise the zophorus above the epistyle is a fourth part less high than the epistyle; but if figures must be designed on it, a fourth part higher than the epistyle, so that the carvings may have authority.

beads.greek: cymatium suae altitudinis partis septimae; proiecturae cymatiûm quantum crassitudo.
beads.english: Its cymatium is a seventh part of its height; the projection of the cymatium as great as its thickness.

beads.greek: [3.5.11] Supra zophorum denticulus est faciendus tam altus quam epistylii media fascia; proiectura eius quantum altitudo.
beads.english: [3.5.11] Above the frieze the dentil is to be made as high as the middle fascia of the epistyle; its projection as much as its height.

beads.greek: intersectio, quae graece μετόπη dicitur, sic est dividenda, uti denticulus altitudinis suae dimidiam partem habeat in fronte, cavus autem intersectionis huius frontis e tribus duas partes; huius cymatium altitudinis eius sextam partem.
beads.english: The cutting (intersectio), which in Greek is called μετόπη (metope), is to be divided in such a way that the dentil has in its face half of its own height, while the hollow of this cutting has two parts out of three of this face; its cymatium a sixth part of its height.

beads.greek: corona cum suo cymatio, praeter simam, quantum media fascia epistylii; proiectura coronae cum denticulo facienda est, quantum erit altitudo a zophoro ad summum coronae cymatium; et omnino omnes ecphorae venustiorem habeant speciem, quae quantum altitudinis tantundem habent proiecturae.
beads.english: The corona with its cymatium, excluding the sima, as much as the middle fascia of the epistyle; the projection of the corona together with the dentil is to be made as much as the height will be from the frieze to the uppermost cymatium of the corona; and in general all ecphorae (projecting members) have a more graceful appearance which have as much projection as they have height.

beads.greek: [3.5.12] Tympani autem, quod est in fastigio, altitudo sic est facienda, uti frons coronae ab extremis cymatiis tota dimetiatur in partes novem et ex eis una pars in medio cacumini tympani constituatur, dum contra epistylia columnarumque hypotrachelia ad perpendiculum respondeant.
beads.english: [3.5.12] But the height of the tympanum, which is in the pediment, is to be made in such a way that the whole face of the corona, from the outermost cymatia, is measured out into nine parts, and of these one part is set at the apex of the tympanum in the middle, provided that they answer perpendicularly over against the epistyles and the hypotrachelia of the columns.

beads.greek: coronaeque supra aequaliter imis praeter simas sunt conlocandae.
beads.english: And the coronae above are to be set equal to the lower ones, except for the simae.

beads.greek: insuper coronas simae, quas Graeci ἐπαιετίδες dicunt, faciendae sunt altiores octava parte coronarum altitudinis.
beads.english: Above the coronae the simae, which the Greeks call ἐπαιετίδες (epaietides), are to be made higher by an eighth part of the height of the coronae.

beads.greek: acroteria angularia tam alta, quantum est tympanum medium, mediana altiora octava parte quam angularia.
beads.english: The corner acroteria as high as the middle of the tympanum, the middle ones an eighth part higher than the corner ones.

beads.greek: [3.5.13] Membra omnia, quae supra capitula columnarum sunt futura, id est epistylia, zophora, coronae, tympana, fastigia, acroteria, inclinanda sunt in fronte suae cuiusque altitudinis parte XII , ideo quod, cum steterimus contra frontes, ab oculo lineae duae si extensae fuerint et una tetigerit imam operis partem, altera summam, quae summam tetigerit, longior fiet.
beads.english: [3.5.13] All the members which are going to be above the capitals of the columns, that is the epistyles, friezes, cornices, tympana, pediments and acroteria, are to be inclined forward at the front by a twelfth part of their own respective height, for this reason: when we have stood facing the fronts, if two lines are extended from the eye and one touches the lowest part of the work, the other the highest, the one that touches the highest will become the longer.

beads.greek: ita quo longior visus linea in superiorem partem procedit, resupinatam facit eius speciem.
beads.english: Thus the further the line of sight proceeds towards the upper part, the more it makes its appearance seem to lean backwards.

beads.greek: cum autem, uti supra scriptum est, in fronte inclinata fuerint, tunc in aspectu videbuntur esse ad perpendiculum et normam.
beads.english: But when, as has been written above, they have been inclined at the front, then to the view they will seem to be true to the plumb-line and the set-square.

beads.greek: [3.5.14] Columnarum striae faciendae sunt XXIIII ita excavatae, uti norma in cavo striae cum fuerit coniecta, circumacta anconibus angulos striarum dextra ac sinistra tangat cacumenque normae circum rotundationem tangendo pervagari possit.
beads.english: [3.5.14] The flutes of the columns are to be made twenty-four in number, hollowed out in such a way that, when a set-square has been placed in the hollow of the flute and swung round on its arms, it touches the corners of the flutes on the right and on the left, and the apex of the set-square can travel around the curvature while touching it.

beads.greek: crassitudines striarum faciendae sunt, quantum adiectio in media columna ex descriptione invenietur.
beads.english: The thicknesses of the flutes are to be made as great as the addition at the middle of the column will be found to be from the diagram.

beads.greek: [3.5.15] In simis, quae supra coronam in lateribus sunt aedium, capita leonina sunt scalpenda, disposita ita , uti contra columnas singulas primum sint designata, cetera aequali modo disposita, uti singula singulis mediis tegulis respondeant.
beads.english: [3.5.15] On the simae which are above the cornice on the sides of temples, lion's heads are to be carved, arranged in such a way that first those opposite each column are marked out, and the rest arranged at equal intervals, so that each corresponds to the middle of each tile.

beads.greek: haec autem, quae erunt contra columnas, perterebrata sint ad canalem, qui excipit e tegulis aquam caelestem; mediana autem sint solida, uti, quae cadit vis aquae per tegulas in canalem, ne deiciatur per intercolumnia neque transeuntes perfundat, sed quae sunt contra columnas, videantur emittere vomentia ructus aquarum ex ore.
beads.english: Those, however, which will be opposite the columns are to be bored through to the channel which receives the rainwater from the tiles; but the intermediate ones are to be solid, so that the mass of water which falls through the tiles into the channel is not thrown down through the intercolumniations and does not drench those passing by, but those which are opposite the columns may appear to vomit forth gushes of water from their mouths.

beads.greek: Aedium ionicarum, quam apertissime potui, dispositiones hoc volumine scripsi; doricarum autem et corinthiarum quae sint proportiones, insequenti libro explicabo.
beads.english: The arrangements of Ionic temples I have set down in this volume as plainly as I could; what the proportions of Doric and Corinthian ones are, I shall explain in the following book.
