beads.greek: LIBER TERTIUS [3.pr.1] Delphicus Apollo Socratem omnium sapientissimum Pythiae responsis est professus.
beads.english: BOOK THREE [3.pr.1] The Delphic Apollo, through the responses of the Pythia, declared Socrates the wisest of all men.

beads.greek: is autem memoratur prudenter doctissimeque dixisse, oportuisse hominum pectora fenestrata et aperta esse, uti non occultos haberent sensus sed patentes ad considerandum.
beads.english: He, moreover, is recorded to have said, prudently and most learnedly, that the breasts of men ought to have been windowed and open, so that they might hold their thoughts not hidden but laid open for examination. Would indeed that the nature of things, following his opinion, had made them unfolded and plainly visible!

beads.greek: utinam vero rerum natura sententiam eius secuta explicata et apparentia ea constituisset!
beads.english: For had it been so, not only would the merits or vices of minds be seen ready to hand, but also the knowledge of the disciplines, placed under the scrutiny of the eyes, would be approved by no uncertain judgements.

beads.greek: si enim ita fuisset, non solum laudes aut vitia animorum ad manum aspicerentur, sed etiam disciplinarum scientiae sub oculorum consideratione subiectae non incertis iudiciis probarentur, sed et doctis et scientibus auctoritas egregia et stabilis adderetur ipsique artifices pellicerent sua prudentia, qui, etiam si non pecunia sint copiosi seu vetustate officinarum habuerint notitiam aut etiam gratia forensi et eloquentia, cum fuerint parati, pro industria studiorum auctoritates possent habere, ut eis, quod profitentur scire, id crederetur.
beads.english: And to the learned and the knowledgeable an eminent and lasting authority would be added, and the artificers themselves would draw clients by their own expertise. Even if they were not abundant in money, nor had gained renown from the long standing of their workshops, nor even through favour in the forum and eloquence, they could, once they were prepared, hold authority in proportion to the diligence of their studies, so that what they profess to know would be believed of them.

beads.greek: igitur quoniam haec non ita, sed uti natura rerum voluit, sunt constituta, non efficitur, ut possint homines obscuratis sub pectoribus ingeniis scientias artificiorum penitus latentes, quemadmodum sint, iudicare.
beads.english: Therefore, since these things have been established not thus, but as the nature of things willed, it does not come about that men, the talents being obscured beneath the breasts, can judge the sciences of the crafts, lying deeply hidden as they are, as they truly are.

beads.greek: [3.pr.2] Maxime autem id animadvertere possumus ab antiquis statuariis et pictoribus, quod ex his, qui dignitatis notas et commendationis gratiam habuerunt, aeterna memoria ad posteritatem sunt permanentes, uti Myron, Polycletus, Phidias, Lysippus ceterique, qui nobilitatem ex arte sunt consecuti.
beads.english: [3.pr.2] We can observe this most of all in the case of the ancient sculptors and painters. Of these, those who held the marks of distinction and the favour of recommendation remain in everlasting memory for posterity: Myron, Polycletus, Phidias, Lysippus and the others who attained renown from their art.

beads.greek: namque ut civitatibus magnis aut regibus aut civibus nobilibus opera fecerunt, ita id sunt adepti.
beads.english: For they obtained this according as they made works for great cities, or for kings, or for noble citizens. But those who were of no less zeal, talent and skill, and who made works no less excellently finished for citizens noble but of humble fortune, attained no memory.

beads.greek: at qui non minore studio et ingenio sollertiaque fuerunt nobilibus et humili fortuna civibus non minus egregie perfecta fecerunt opera, nullam memoriam sunt adsecuti, quod hi non ab industria neque artis sollertia sed a felicitate fuerunt deserti, ut Hegias Atheniensis, Chion Corinthius, Myagrus Phocaeus, Pharax Ephesius, Boedas Byzantius etiamque alii plures.
beads.english: This was because they were abandoned not by industry nor by skill in their art but by good fortune: such were Hegias of Athens, Chion of Corinth, Myagrus of Phocaea, Pharax of Ephesus, Boedas of Byzantium, and many others besides. Likewise, no less, the painters, such as Aristomenes of Thasos, Polycles and Androcydes of Cyzicus, Theo of Magnesia and the rest.

beads.greek: non minus item pictores, uti Aristomenes Thasius, Polycles et Androcydes Cyzice ni, Theo Magnes ceterique, quos neque industria neque artis studium neque sollertia defecit, sed aut rei familiaris exiguitas aut inbecillitas fortunae seu in ambitione certationis contrariorum superatio obstitit eorum dignitati.
beads.english: Neither industry nor zeal for their art nor skill failed them. Instead, their standing was obstructed either by the slenderness of their private means, or by the weakness of their fortune, or, in the canvassing of competition, by their being overcome by their opponents.

beads.greek: [3.pr.3] Nec tamen est admirandum, si propter ignotitiam artis virtutes obscurantur, sed maxime indignandum, cum etiam saepe eblandiatur gratia conviviorum a veris iudiciis falsam probationem.
beads.english: [3.pr.3] Yet it is not to be wondered at if, through ignorance of the art, merits are obscured; but it is most of all a matter for indignation when, as often happens, the favour won at banquets coaxes a false approval from genuine judgements.

beads.greek: ergo, uti Socrati placuit, si ita sensus et sententiae scientiaeque disciplinis auctae perspicuae et perlucidae fuissent, non gratia neque ambitio valeret, sed si qui veris certisque laboribus doctrinarum pervenissent ad scientiam summam, eis ultro opera traderentur.
beads.english: Therefore, as Socrates held, if men's feelings and opinions, and their knowledge increased by the branches of learning, had been thus transparent and clearly visible, neither favour nor canvassing would prevail; rather, if any had attained the highest knowledge through true and sure labours in their studies, commissions would be offered to them unasked.

beads.greek: quoniam autem ea non sunt inlustria neque apparentia in aspectu, ut putamus oportuisse, et animadverto potius indoctos quam doctos gratia superare, non esse certandum iudicans cum indoctis ambitione, potius his praeceptis editis ostendam nostrae scientiae virtutem.
beads.english: But since these things are not plain nor apparent to view, as we think they ought to have been, and I observe that the unlearned rather than the learned prevail through favour, judging that one ought not to contend with the unlearned in canvassing, I shall rather show the excellence of our knowledge by publishing these precepts.

beads.greek: [3.pr.4] Itaque, imperator, in primo volumine tibi de arte et quas habeat ea virtutes quibusque disciplinis oporteat esse auctum architectum, exposui et subieci causas, quid ita earum oporteat eum esse peritum, rationesque summae architecturae partitione distribui finitionibusque terminavi.
beads.english: [3.pr.4] Accordingly, Imperator, in the first book I set out for you the art, what excellences it possesses, and with what branches of learning the architect ought to be equipped, and I added the reasons why he ought to be skilled in them; and I distributed the principles of architecture as a whole by division and bounded them by definitions.

beads.greek: deinde, quod erat primum et necessarium, de moenibus, quemadmodum eligantur loci salubres, ratiocinationibus explicui, ventique qui sint et e quibus regionibus singuli spirant, deformationibus grammicis ostendi, platearumque et vicorum uti emendate fiant distributiones in moenibus, docui et ita finitionem primo volumine constitui.
beads.english: Next, as was first and necessary, I explained by reasoned arguments, concerning city walls, how healthy sites are to be chosen; and I showed by linear diagrams what the winds are and from which quarters each of them blows; and I taught how the layouts of the avenues and streets within the walls are to be correctly made; and thus I set the limit of the first book.

beads.greek: item in secundo de materia, quas habeat in operibus utilitates et quibus virtutibus e natura rerum est comparata, peregi.
beads.english: Likewise in the second I treated of building material: what advantages it has in works, and with what properties it has been furnished by the nature of things.

beads.greek: nunc in tertio de deorum inmortalium aedibus sacris dicam et, uti oportet, perscriptas exponam.
beads.english: Now in the third I shall speak of the sacred temples of the immortal gods and set them out, fully described, as is proper.

beads.greek: [3.1.1] Aedium compositio constat ex symmetria, cuius rationem diligentissime architecti tenere debent.
beads.english: [3.1.1] The composition of temples consists in symmetry, the principle of which architects ought to hold to most diligently.

beads.greek: ea autem paritur a proportione, quae graece ἀναλογία dicitur.
beads.english: This, moreover, is produced by proportion, which in Greek is called ἀναλογία.

beads.greek: proportio est ratae partis membrorum in omni opere totiusque commodulatio, ex qua ratio efficitur symmetriarum.
beads.english: Proportion is the commodulation, by a fixed part, of the members in every work and of the whole, from which the principle of symmetries is brought about.

beads.greek: namque non potest aedis ulla sine symmetria atque proportione rationem habere compositionis, nisi uti hominis bene figurati membrorum habuerit exactam rationem.
beads.english: For no temple can have a principle of composition without symmetry and proportion, unless it has an exact relation of its members like that of a well-shaped man.

beads.greek: [3.1.2] Corpus enim hominis ita natura composuit, uti os capitis a mento ad frontem summam et radices imas capilli esset decimae partis, item manus pansa ab articulo ad extremum medium digitum tantundem, caput a mento ad summum verticem octavae, cum cervicibus imis ab summo pectore ad imas radices capillorum sextae, a medio pectore ad summum verticem quartae.
beads.english: [3.1.2] For nature has so composed the body of a man that the face, from the chin to the top of the forehead and the lowest roots of the hair, is a tenth part; likewise the open hand, from the wrist to the tip of the middle finger, just as much; the head, from the chin to the top of the crown, an eighth; from the top of the chest, together with the base of the neck, to the lowest roots of the hair, a sixth; from the middle of the chest to the top of the crown, a fourth.

beads.greek: ipsius autem oris altitudinis tertia est pars ab imo mento ad imas nares, nasum ab imis naribus ad finem mediûm superciliorum tantundem, ab ea fine ad imas radices capilli frons efficitur item tertiae partis.
beads.english: Of the height of the face itself, moreover, one third is from the bottom of the chin to the bottom of the nostrils; the nose, from the bottom of the nostrils to the boundary at the middle of the eyebrows, just as much; from that boundary to the lowest roots of the hair the forehead is formed, likewise of a third part.

beads.greek: pes vero altitudinis corporis sextae, cubitum quartae, pectus item quartae.
beads.english: The foot, indeed, is a sixth of the height of the body, the cubit a fourth, the chest likewise a fourth.

beads.greek: reliqua quoque membra suas habent commensus proportiones, quibus etiam antiqui pictores et statuarii nobiles usi magnas et infinitas laudes sunt adsecuti.
beads.english: The remaining members also have their own proportions of commensuration, by making use of which the ancient painters and noble sculptors also attained great and boundless praise.

beads.greek: [3.1.3] Similiter vero sacrarum aedium membra ad universam totius magnitudinis summam ex partibus singulis convenientissimum debent habere commensus responsum.
beads.english: [3.1.3] In the same way, the members of sacred temples ought to have, from their individual parts, a most fitting correspondence of commensuration to the general sum of the whole magnitude.

beads.greek: item corporis centrum medium naturaliter est umbilicus.
beads.english: Again, the central midpoint of the body is by nature the navel.

beads.greek: namque si homo conlocatus fuerit supinus manibus et pedibus pansis circinique conlocatum centrum in umbilico eius, circumagendo rotundationem utrarumque manuum et pedum digiti linea tangentur.
beads.english: For if a man is laid on his back with hands and feet spread out, and the centre of a pair of compasses is set on his navel, then in drawing the circle round, the fingers and toes of both hands and feet will be touched by the line.

beads.greek: non minus quemadmodum schema rotundationis in corpore efficitur, item quadrata designatio in eo invenietur.
beads.english: And no less than a circular figure is produced in the body, so also a square delineation will be found in it.

beads.greek: nam si a pedibus imis ad summum caput mensum erit eaque mensura relata fuerit ad manus pansas, invenietur eadem latitudo uti altitudo, quemadmodum areae, quae ad normam sunt quadratae.
beads.english: For if one measures from the soles of the feet to the top of the head, and that measure is transferred to the outstretched hands, the breadth will be found to be the same as the height, as in areas that are squared by the set-square.

beads.greek: [3.1.4] Ergo si ita natura composuit corpus hominis, uti proportionibus membra ad summam figurationem eius respondeant, cum causa constituisse videntur antiqui, ut etiam in operum perfectionibus singulorum membrorum ad universam figurae speciem habeant commensus exactionem.
beads.english: [3.1.4] Therefore, if nature has so composed the human body that its members correspond in their proportions to its entire configuration, the ancients appear to have laid it down with good reason that in the completion of works also there should be an exactness of commensuration of the individual members to the general appearance of the figure.

beads.greek: igitur cum in omnibus operibus ordines traderent, maxime in aedibus deorum, quod eorum operum et laudes et culpae aeternae solent permanere.
beads.english: Accordingly, while they handed down orderly arrangements for all works, they did so above all for the temples of the gods, because the praise and the blame for those works are wont to endure forever.

non minus quemadmodum schema rotundationis in corpore efficitur, item quadrata designatio in eo invenietur.
nam si a pedibus imis ad summum caput mensum erit eaque mensura relata fuerit ad manus pansas, invenietur eadem latitudo uti altitudo, quemadmodum areae, quae ad normam sunt quadratae.

[3.1.4] Ergo si ita natura composuit corpus hominis, uti proportionibus membra ad summam figurationem eius respondeant, cum causa constituisse videntur antiqui, ut etiam in operum perfectionibus singulorum membrorum ad universam figurae speciem habeant commensus exactionem.
igitur cum in omnibus operibus ordines traderent, maxime in aedibus deorum, quod eorum operum et laudes et culpae aeternae solent permanere.
english_sentences: [3.1.3] In the same way, the members of sacred temples ought to have, from their individual parts, a most fitting correspondence of commensuration to the general sum of the whole magnitude.
Again, the central midpoint of the body is by nature the navel.

For if a man is laid on his back with hands and feet spread out, and the centre of a pair of compasses is set on his navel, then in drawing the circle round, the fingers and toes of both hands and feet will be touched by the line.
And no less than a circular figure is produced in the body, so also a square delineation will be found in it.

For if one measures from the soles of the feet to the top of the head, and that measure is transferred to the outstretched hands, the breadth will be found to be the same as the height, as in areas that are squared by the set-square.

[3.1.4] Therefore, if nature has so composed the human body that its members correspond in their proportions to its entire configuration, the ancients appear to have laid it down with good reason that in the completion of works also there should be an exactness of commensuration of the individual members to the general appearance of the figure.
Accordingly, while they handed down orderly arrangements for all works, they did so above all for the temples of the gods, because the praise and the blame for those works are wont to endure forever.

beads.greek: [3.1.5] Nec minus mensurarum rationes, quae in omnibus operibus videntur necessariae esse, ex corporis membris collegerunt, uti digitum, palmum, pedem, cubitum, et eas distribuerunt in perfectum numerum, quem Graeci τέλειον dicunt.
beads.english: [3.1.5] No less did they gather from the members of the body the principles of the measures which appear to be necessary in all works, such as the digit, the palm, the foot and the cubit, and they distributed these into the perfect number, which the Greeks call τέλειον.

beads.greek: perfectum autem antiqui instituerunt numerum qui decem dicitur; namque ex manibus digitorum numero est inventus.
beads.english: Now the ancients established as perfect the number that is called ten; for it was found from the number of the fingers on the hands.

beads.greek: si autem in utrisque palmis ex articulis ab natura decem sunt perfecti, etiam Platoni placuit esse eum numerum ea re perfectum, quod ex X singularibus rebus, quae μονάδες apud Graecos dicuntur, perficitur decusis.
beads.english: And if from the joints on both palms ten are completed by nature, it pleased Plato also that this number is perfect for the reason that the decussis is completed from ten single things, which among the Greeks are called μονάδες.

beads.greek: simul autem undecim aut duodecim sunt facti, quod superaverint, non possunt esse perfecti, donec ad alterum decusis perveniant; singulares enim res particulae sunt eius numeri.
beads.english: But as soon as eleven or twelve are made, because they have gone beyond it, they cannot be perfect until they arrive at the second decussis; for the single things are small parts of that number.

beads.greek: [3.1.6] Mathematici vero contra disputantes ea re perfectum dixerunt esse numerum qui sex dicitur, quod is numerus habet partitiones eorum rationibus sex numero convenientes sic: sextantem unum, trientes duo, semissem tria, besem quem δίμοιρον dicunt quattuor, quintarium quem πεντάμοιρον dicunt quinque, perfectum sex.
beads.english: [3.1.6] The mathematicians, however, arguing to the contrary, have said that the number called six is perfect, for this reason: that this number has divisions which, by their ratios, agree with the number six, thus: the sextans is one, the trientes two, the semis three, the bes, which they call dimoiros, four, the quintarius, which they call pentamoiros, five, the perfect six.

beads.greek: cum ad duplicationem crescat, supra sex adiecto asse ἔφεκτον ; cum facta sunt octo, quod est tertia adiecta, tertiarium alterum, qui ἐπίτριτος dicitur; dimidia adiecta cum facta sunt novem, sesquialterum, qui ἡμιόλιος appellatur; duabus partibus additis et decusis facto bes alterum, quem ἐπιδίμοιρον vocitant; in undecim numero quod adiecti sunt quinque, quintarium, quem ἐπίπεμπτον dicunt; duodecim autem, quod ex duobus numeris simplicibus est effectus, διπλάσιονα .
beads.english: As it grows towards doubling, when an as is added above six, it is ephekton; when eight has been reached, because a third has been added, it is the second tertiarius, which is called epitritos; when nine has been reached by the addition of a half, it is the sesquialter, which is named hemiolios; when two parts have been added and ten has been made, it is the second bes, which they call epidimoiros; in the number eleven, because five have been added, it is the quintarius, which they call epipemptos; twelve, however, because it is produced from two simple numbers, is diplasion.

beads.greek: [3.1.7] Non minus etiam, quod pes hominis altitudinis sextam habet partem, (ita etiam, ex eo quod perficitur pedum numero corporis altitudo, veteribus columnis basis scapi elata sexies altitudines terminavit) eum perfectum constituerunt, cubitumque animadverterunt ex sex palmis constare digitisque XXIIII .
beads.english: [3.1.7] No less also, because a man's foot is the sixth part of his height (and so too, from the fact that the height of the body is completed by the number of feet, the base of the shaft in ancient columns, raised six times, determined their heights), they established that number as perfect, and they observed that the cubit consists of six palms and twenty-four digits.

beads.greek: ex eo etiam videntur civitates Graecorum fecisse, quemadmodum cubitus est sex palmorum, in drachma, qua nummo uterentur, aereos signatos uti asses ex aequo sex, quos obolos appellant, quadrantesque obolorum, quae alii dichalca, nonnulli trichalca dicunt, pro digitis viginti quattuor in drachma constituisse.
beads.english: From this, too, the states of the Greeks seem to have acted likewise: just as the cubit is of six palms, so in the drachma, which they used as coin, they established stamped bronze pieces, like asses, six of equal value, which they call obols; and quarters of obols, which some call dichalka and others trichalka, they established to the number of twenty-four in the drachma, corresponding to the digits.

beads.greek: [3.1.8] Nostri autem primo fecerunt perfectum antiquum numerum et in denario denos aeris constituerunt, et ea re compositio nominis ad hodiernum diem denarium retinet.
beads.english: [3.1.8] Our people, however, at first made the ancient number perfect and established ten bronze pieces in the denarius, and for that reason the composition of the name retains 'denarius' to the present day.

beads.greek: etiamque quarta pars quod efficiebatur ex duobus assibus et tertio semisse, sestertium vocitaverunt.
beads.english: And also its fourth part, because it was made up of two asses and the third a half-as, they called the sestertius.

beads.greek: postea autem quam animadverterunt utrosque numeros esse perfectos, et sex et decem, utrosque in unum coiecerunt et fecerunt perfectissimum decusis sexis.
beads.english: But later, when they observed that both numbers were perfect, both six and ten, they combined both into one and made the most perfect number, sixteen.

beads.greek: huius autem rei auctorem invenerunt pedem.
beads.english: Of this they found the foot to be the origin.

beads.greek: e cubito enim cum dempti sunt palmi duo, relinquitur pes quattuor palmorum, palmus autem habet quattuor digitos.
beads.english: For when two palms are taken from the cubit, there remains the foot of four palms, and a palm has four digits.

beads.greek: ita efficitur, ut habeat pes sedecim digitos et totidem asses aeracius denarius.
beads.english: Thus it comes about that the foot has sixteen digits, and the bronze denarius just as many asses.

beads.greek: [3.1.9] Ergo si convenit ex articulis hominis numerum inventum esse et ex membris separatis ad universam corporis speciem ratae partis commensus fieri responsum, relinquitur, ut suspiciamus eos, qui etiam aedes deorum inmortalium constituentes ita membra operum ordinaverunt, ut proportionibus et symmetriis separatae atque universae convenientes efficerentur eorum distributiones.
beads.english: [3.1.9] Therefore, if it is agreed that number was discovered from the joints of the human body, and that from the separate members there arises a correspondence of commensuration, by a fixed part, to the whole appearance of the body, it remains for us to look up to those who, when establishing the temples of the immortal gods as well, so ordered the members of the works that, by means of proportions and symmetries, their distributions were made concordant both in their separate parts and as a whole.

beads.greek: [3.2.1] Aedium autem principia sunt, e quibus constat figurarum aspectus, ea: primum in antis, quod graece ναὸς ἐν παραστάσιν dicitur, deinde prostylos, amphiprostylos, peripteros, pseudodipteros, dipteros , hypaethros.
beads.english: [3.2.1] The basic types of temples, from which the appearance of their forms is constituted, are these: first, in antis, which in Greek is called ναὸς ἐν παραστάσιν; then prostyle, amphiprostyle, peripteral, pseudodipteral, dipteral, hypaethral.

beads.greek: horum exprimuntur formationes his rationibus.
beads.english: The configurations of these are expressed according to the following principles.

beads.greek: [3.2.2] In antis erit aedes, cum habebit in fronte antas parietum, qui cellam circumcludunt, et inter antas in medio columnas duas supraque fastigium symmetria ea conlocatum, quae in hoc libro fuerit perscripta.
beads.english: [3.2.2] A temple will be in antis when it has at the front the antae of the walls that enclose the cella, and between the antae, in the middle, two columns, and above them a pediment placed according to that symmetry which will have been set down in this book.

beads.greek: huius autem exemplar erit ad Tres Fortunas extribus quod est proxime portam Collinam.
beads.english: An example of this will be at the Three Fortunes, the one of the three that is nearest the Colline Gate.

beads.greek: [3.2.3] Prostylos omnia habet quemadmodum in antis, columnas autem contra antas angulares duas supraque epistylia, quemadmodum et in antis, et dextra ac sinistra in versuris singula.
beads.english: [3.2.3] The prostyle has everything as the temple in antis has, but opposite the antae it has two corner columns, and above them architraves, as also in the temple in antis, and one each to right and left at the returns.

beads.greek: huius exemplar est in insula Tiberina in aede Iovis et Fauni.
beads.english: An example of this is on the Tiber Island, in the temple of Jupiter and Faunus.

beads.greek: [3.2.4] amphiprostylos omnia habet ea, quae prostylos, praetereaque habet in postico ad eundem modum columnas et fastigium.
beads.english: [3.2.4] The amphiprostyle has everything that the prostyle has, and besides this it has at the back, in the same manner, columns and a pediment.

beads.greek: [3.2.5] Peripteros autem erit, quae habebit in fronte et postico senas columnas, in lateribus cum angularibus undenas.
beads.english: [3.2.5] The peripteral temple, moreover, will be one that has six columns each on the front and at the back, and eleven each on the sides, counting the corner columns.

beads.greek: ita autem sint hae columnae conlocatae, ut intercolumnii latitudinis intervallum sit a parietibus circum ad extremos ordines columnarum, habeatque ambulationem circa cellam aedis, quemadmodum est sine postico in porticu Metelli Iovis Statoris Hermodori et Mariana Honoris et Virtutis a Mucio facta.
beads.english: These columns are to be so placed that there is an interval of the width of an intercolumniation from the walls round about to the outermost rows of columns, and it is to have a walkway around the cella of the temple, as there is, without a back portion, in the portico of Metellus, the temple of Jupiter Stator by Hermodorus, and in the Marian temple of Honour and Virtue built by Mucius.

beads.greek: [3.2.6] Pseudodipteros autem sic conlocatur, ut in fronte et postico sint columnae octonae, in lateribus cum angularibus quinae denae.
beads.english: [3.2.6] The pseudodipteros is laid out so that there are eight columns each in the front and in the posticum, and fifteen each on the sides, counting the corner columns.

beads.greek: sint autem parietes cellae contra quaternas columnas medianas in fronte et postico.
beads.english: The walls of the cella are to stand opposite the four middle columns in the front and in the posticum.

beads.greek: ita duorum intercolumniorum et imae crassitudinis columnae spatium erit ab parietibus circa ad extremos ordines columnarum.
beads.english: Thus there will be a space of two intercolumniations plus the thickness of a column at its base, from the walls round to the outermost rows of columns.

beads.greek: huius exemplar Romae non est, sed Magnesiae Dianae Hermogenis Alabandei et Apollinis a Menesthe facta.
beads.english: There is no example of this at Rome, but there is one at Magnesia, the temple of Diana by Hermogenes of Alabanda, and the temple of Apollo built by Menesthes.

beads.greek: [3.2.7] Dipteros autem octastylos et pronao et postico, sed circa aedem duplices habet ordines columnarum, uti est aedis Quirini dorica et Ephesi Dianae ionica a Chersiphrone constituta.
beads.english: [3.2.7] The dipteros is octastyle both in the pronaos and in the posticum, but around the temple it has double rows of columns, as is the Doric temple of Quirinus and the Ionic temple of Diana at Ephesus, set up by Chersiphron.

beads.greek: [3.2.8] Hypaethros vero decastylos est in pronao et postico.
beads.english: [3.2.8] The hypaethros is decastyle in the pronaos and in the posticum.

beads.greek: reliqua omnia eadem habet quae dipteros, sed interiore parte columnas in altitudine duplices, remotas a parietibus ad circumitionem ut porticus peristyliorum.
beads.english: In all other respects it has the same features as the dipteros, but in the interior it has columns doubled in height, that is in two tiers, set back from the walls so as to allow a passage round, like the porticoes of peristyles.

beads.greek: medium autem sub divo est sine tecto.
beads.english: The middle is open to the sky, without a roof.

beads.greek: aditus valvarum ex utraque parte in pronao et postico.
beads.english: There are entrances with folding doors at either end, in the pronaos and in the posticum.

beads.greek: huius item exemplar Romae non est, sed Athenis octastylos ex templo Olympio.
beads.english: Of this too there is no example at Rome, but at Athens there is the octastyle in the Olympian temple precinct.

[3.2.7] The dipteros is octastyle both in the pronaos and in the posticum, but around the temple it has double rows of columns, as is the Doric temple of Quirinus and the Ionic temple of Diana at Ephesus, set up by Chersiphron.
[3.2.8] The hypaethros is decastyle in the pronaos and in the posticum.

In all other respects it has the same features as the dipteros, but in the interior it has columns doubled in height, that is in two tiers, set back from the walls so as to allow a passage round, like the porticoes of peristyles.
The middle is open to the sky, without a roof.
There are entrances with folding doors at either end, in the pronaos and in the posticum.
Of this too there is no example at Rome, but at Athens there is the octastyle in the Olympian temple precinct.

beads.greek: [3.3.1] Species autem aedium sunt quinque, quarum ea sunt vocabula: pycnostylos, id est crebris columnis, systylos paulo remissioribus, diastylos amplius quam oportet inter se diductis, araeostylos spatiis intercolumniorum patentibus rare, eustylos intervallorum iusta distributione.
beads.english: [3.3.1] There are, moreover, five species of temples, whose names are these: pycnostyle, that is, with close-set columns; systyle, with columns somewhat more widely spaced; diastyle, with columns set apart from one another more widely than is proper; araeostyle, with the spaces of the intercolumniations lying open sparsely; eustyle, with a correct distribution of the intervals.

beads.greek: [3.3.2] Ergo pycnostylos est, cuius intercolumnio unius et dimidiatae columnae crassitudo interponi potest, quemadmodum est divi Iulii et in Caesaris foro Veneris et si quae aliae sic sunt compositae.
beads.english: [3.3.2] The pycnostyle, then, is the temple in whose intercolumniation the thickness of one and a half columns can be interposed, as is the temple of the Deified Julius, and that of Venus in the Forum of Caesar, and any others that are composed in this way.

beads.greek: item systylos est, in qua duarum columnarum crassitudo in intercolumnio poterit conlocari, et spirarum plinthides aeque magnae sint ei spatio, quod fuerit inter duas plinthides, quemadmodum est Fortunae Equestris ad theatrum lapideum reliquaeque, quae eisdem rationibus sunt compositae.
beads.english: Likewise the systyle is the temple in which the thickness of two columns can be placed in the intercolumniation, and the plinths of the bases are equal in size to the space between two plinths, as is the temple of Fortuna Equestris by the stone theatre, and the others that are composed on the same principles.

beads.greek: [3.3.3] Haec utraque genera vitiosum habent usum.
beads.english: [3.3.3] Both of these kinds are faulty in use.

beads.greek: matres enim familiarum cum ad supplicationem gradibus ascendunt, non possunt per intercolumnia amplexae adire, nisi ordines fecerint; item valvarum aspectus abstruditur columnarum crebritate ipsaque signa obscurantur; item circa aedem propter angustias inpediuntur ambulationes.
beads.english: For when the matrons go up the steps for a supplication, they cannot pass through the intercolumniations arm in arm unless they form files; likewise the view of the folding doors is shut off by the closeness of the columns, and the statues themselves are obscured; likewise the walks around the temple are hindered by the narrowness.

beads.greek: [3.3.4] Diastyli autem haec erit compositio, cum trium columnarum crassitudinem intercolumnio interponere possumus, tamquam est Apollinis et Dianae aedis.
beads.english: [3.3.4] The composition of the diastyle, on the other hand, will be this: when we can set the thickness of three columns into an intercolumniation, as is the case with the temple of Apollo and Diana.

beads.greek: haec dispositio hanc habet difficultatem, quod epistylia propter intervallorum magnitudinem franguntur.
beads.english: This arrangement has this difficulty, that the architraves break because of the size of the intervals.

beads.greek: [3.3.5] In araeostylis autem nec lapideis nec marmoreis epistyliis uti datur, sed inponendae de materia trabes perpetuae.
beads.english: [3.3.5] In araeostyle temples, moreover, it is not possible to use architraves of stone or of marble, but continuous beams of timber must be laid on.

beads.greek: et ipsarum aedium species sunt varicae, barycephalae, humiles, latae, ornanturque signis fictilibus aut aereis inauratis earum fastigia tuscanico more, uti est ad Circum Maximum Cereris et Herculis Pompeiani, item Capitolii.
beads.english: And the appearance of these temples is splay-legged, top-heavy, low and broad, and their pediments are adorned in the Tuscan manner with statues of terracotta or of gilded bronze, as is the temple of Ceres at the Circus Maximus, and that of Pompey's Hercules, and likewise that of the Capitol.

beads.greek: [3.3.6] Reddenda nunc est eustyli ratio, quae maxime probabilis et ad usum et ad speciem et ad firmitatem rationes habet explicatas.
beads.english: [3.3.6] We must now give the principle of the eustyle, which is the most commendable and has its principles worked out with regard to use, to appearance and to strength.

beads.greek: namque facienda sunt in intervallis spatia duarum columnarum et quartae partis columnae crassitudinis, mediumque intercolumnium unum, quod erit in fronte, alterum, quod in postico, trium columnarum crassitudine.
beads.english: For the spaces in the intervals are to be made of two column-thicknesses and a quarter of a column's thickness, and the middle intercolumniation, one on the front and the other on the rear, of three column-thicknesses.

beads.greek: sic enim habebit et figurationis aspectum venustum et aditus usum sine inpeditionibus et circa cellam ambulatio auctoritatem.
beads.english: In this way the building will have a graceful appearance in its design, the use of the entrance without obstructions, and dignity in the walk around the cella.

beads.greek: [3.3.7] Huius autem rei ratio explicabitur sic.
beads.english: [3.3.7] The principle of this arrangement will be set out as follows.

beads.greek: frons loci quae in aede constituta fuerit, si tetrastylos facienda fuerit, dividatur in partes XI S praeter crepidines et proiecturas spirarum; si sex erit columnarum, in partes XVIII ; si octastylos constituetur, dividatur in XXIV et semissem.
beads.english: The front of the site established for the temple, if a tetrastyle is to be built, is to be divided into 11½ parts, excluding the crepidines and the projections of the bases; if it is to be of six columns, into 18 parts; if an octastyle is to be set up, it is to be divided into 24½.

beads.greek: item ex his partibus sive tetrastyli sive hexastyli sive octastyli una pars sumatur, eaque erit modulus.
beads.english: Likewise, of these parts, whether of the tetrastyle, the hexastyle or the octastyle, one part is to be taken, and this will be the module.

beads.greek: cuius moduli unus erit crassitudinis columnarum.
beads.english: One of these modules will be the thickness of the columns.

beads.greek: intercolumnia singula, praeter media, modulorum duorum et moduli quartae partis; mediana in fronte et postico singula ternûm modulorum.
beads.english: Each of the intercolumniations, except the middle ones, is to be of two modules and a quarter of a module; the middle ones, on the front and the rear, one each, of three modules apiece.

beads.greek: ipsarum columnarum altitudo modulorum VIIII et dimidiae moduli partis.
beads.english: The height of the columns themselves is to be of 9½ modules.

beads.greek: ita ex ea divisione intercolumnia altitudinesque columnarum habebunt iustam rationem.
beads.english: Thus, from this division, the intercolumniations and the heights of the columns will have a correct proportion.

In this way the building will have a graceful appearance in its design, the use of the entrance without obstructions, and dignity in the walk around the cella.
[3.3.7] The principle of this arrangement will be set out as follows.

The front of the site established for the temple, if a tetrastyle is to be built, is to be divided into 11½ parts, excluding the crepidines and the projections of the bases; if it is to be of six columns, into 18 parts; if an octastyle is to be set up, it is to be divided into 24½.
Likewise, of these parts, whether of the tetrastyle, the hexastyle or the octastyle, one part is to be taken, and this will be the module.
One of these modules will be the thickness of the columns.
Each of the intercolumniations, except the middle ones, is to be of two modules and a quarter of a module; the middle ones, on the front and the rear, one each, of three modules apiece.
The height of the columns themselves is to be of 9½ modules.
Thus, from this division, the intercolumniations and the heights of the columns will have a correct proportion.

beads.greek: [3.3.8] Huius exemplar Romae nullum habemus, sed in Asia Teo hexastylon Liberi Patris.
beads.english: [3.3.8] Of this we have no example at Rome, but in Asia there is at Teos the hexastyle temple of Father Liber.

beads.greek: Eas autem symmetrias constituit Hermogenes, qui etiam primus invenit octastylon pseudodipterive rationem.
beads.english: These symmetries, moreover, were established by Hermogenes, who was also the first to devise the scheme of the octastyle, that is, of the pseudodipteral temple.

beads.greek: ex dipteri enim aedis symmetria distulit interiores ordines columnarum XXXIV eaque ratione sumptus operasque compendii fecit.
beads.english: For he removed from the symmetry of the dipteral temple the inner rows of columns, thirty-four in number, and by this method made a saving of expense and labour.

beads.greek: is in medio ambulationi laxamentum egregie circa cellam fecit de aspectuque nihil inminuit, sed sine desiderio supervacuorum conservavit auctoritatem totius operis distributione.
beads.english: In the middle he admirably created spaciousness for the walkway around the cella, and took nothing away from its appearance; rather, without any want of the superfluous elements being felt, he preserved the dignity of the whole work by its layout.

beads.greek: [3.3.9] Pteromatos enim ratio et columnarum circum aedem dispositio ideo est inventa, ut aspectus propter asperitatem intercolumniorum habeat auctoritatem, praeterea, si ex improviso imbrium aquae vis occupaverit et intercluserit hominum multitudinem, ut habeat in aede circaque cellam cum laxamento liberam moram.
beads.english: [3.3.9] For the scheme of the pteroma and the disposition of columns around a temple were devised so that the appearance might have dignity on account of the roughness (asperitatem) of the intercolumniations. Further, if a violent downpour of rain should unexpectedly overtake and shut in a crowd of people, they might have free room to wait, with spaciousness, within the temple and around the cella.

beads.greek: haec autem ut explicantur in pseudodipteris aedium dispositionibus!
beads.english: How well these things are worked out in the pseudodipteral arrangements of temples!

beads.greek: quare videtur acuta magnaque sollertia effectus operum Hermogenes fecisse reliquisseque fontes, unde posteri possent haurire disciplinarum rationes.
beads.english: Hence Hermogenes seems to have achieved the effects of his works with acute and great ingenuity, and to have left behind sources from which posterity might draw the principles of the disciplines.

For he removed from the symmetry of the dipteral temple the inner rows of columns, thirty-four in number, and by this method made a saving of expense and labour.

In the middle he admirably created spaciousness for the walkway around the cella, and took nothing away from its appearance; rather, without any want of the superfluous elements being felt, he preserved the dignity of the whole work by its layout.

[3.3.9] For the scheme of the pteroma and the disposition of columns around a temple were devised so that the appearance might have dignity on account of the roughness (asperitatem) of the intercolumniations.
Further, if a violent downpour of rain should unexpectedly overtake and shut in a crowd of people, they might have free room to wait, with spaciousness, within the temple and around the cella.
How well these things are worked out in the pseudodipteral arrangements of temples!
Hence Hermogenes seems to have achieved the effects of his works with acute and great ingenuity, and to have left behind sources from which posterity might draw the principles of the disciplines.

beads.greek: [3.3.10] Aedibus araeostylis columnae sic sunt faciendae, uti crassitudines earum sint partis octavae ad altitudines.
beads.english: [3.3.10] In araeostyle temples the columns are to be made so that their thicknesses are one eighth part of their heights.

beads.greek: item in diastylo dimetienda est altitudo columnae in partes octo et dimidiam, et unius partis columnae crassitudo conlocetur.
beads.english: Likewise in the diastyle the height of the column is to be measured off into eight and a half parts, and the thickness of the column is to be set at one part.

beads.greek: in systylo altitudo dividatur in novem et dimidiam partem, et ex eis una ad crassitudinem columnae detur.
beads.english: In the systyle let the height be divided into nine and a half parts, and of these let one be given to the thickness of the column.

beads.greek: item in pycnostylo dividenda est altitudo in partes decem, et eius una pars facienda est columnae crassitudo.
beads.english: Likewise in the pycnostyle the height is to be divided into ten parts, and one part of it is to be made the thickness of the column.

beads.greek: eustyli autem aedis columnae, uti systyli, in novem partes altitudo dividatur et dimidiam partem, et eius una pars constituatur in crassitudine imi scapi.
beads.english: For the columns of a eustyle temple, as for those of the systyle, let the height be divided into nine and a half parts, and let one part of it be fixed as the thickness of the bottom of the shaft.

beads.greek: ita habebitur pro rata parte intercolumniorum ratio.
beads.english: In this way the system of the intercolumniations will be maintained in due proportion.

beads.greek: [3.3.11] Quemadmodum enim crescunt spatia inter columnas, proportionibus adaugendae sunt crassitudines scaporum.
beads.english: [3.3.11] For in the same measure as the spaces between the columns increase, the thicknesses of the shafts must be enlarged in proportion.

beads.greek: namque si in araeostylo nona aut decima pars crassitudinis fuerit, tenuis et exilis apparebit, ideo quod per latitudinem intercolumniorum aer consumit et inminuit aspectu scaporum crassitudinem.
beads.english: If in the araeostyle the thickness were a ninth or a tenth part, the column will appear thin and meagre, because through the breadth of the intercolumniations the air consumes and diminishes the apparent thickness of the shafts.

beads.greek: contra vero pycnostylis si octava pars crassitudinis fuerit, propter crebritatem et angustias intercolumniorum tumidam et invenustam efficiet speciem.
beads.english: Conversely, in pycnostyles, if the thickness were an eighth part, the closeness and narrowness of the intercolumniations will produce a swollen and ungraceful appearance.

beads.greek: itaque generis operis oportet persequi symmetrias.
beads.english: Therefore one must follow the symmetries proper to the kind of work.

beads.greek: etiamque angulares columnae crassiores faciendae sunt ex sua diametro quinquagesima parte, quod eae ab aere circumciduntur et graciliores videntur esse aspicientibus.
beads.english: Moreover, the corner columns are to be made thicker by a fiftieth part of their own diameter, because they are cut around by the air and appear more slender to those looking at them.

beads.greek: ergo quod oculus fallit, ratiocinatione est exaequandum.
beads.english: Therefore where the eye deceives, the deficiency must be made good by calculation.

english_sentences: [3.3.10] In araeostyle temples the columns are to be made so that their thicknesses are one eighth part of their heights.
Likewise in the diastyle the height of the column is to be measured off into eight and a half parts, and the thickness of the column is to be set at one part.
In the systyle let the height be divided into nine and a half parts, and of these let one be given to the thickness of the column.
Likewise in the pycnostyle the height is to be divided into ten parts, and one part of it is to be made the thickness of the column.
For the columns of a eustyle temple, as for those of the systyle, let the height be divided into nine and a half parts, and let one part of it be fixed as the thickness of the bottom of the shaft.
In this way the system of the intercolumniations will be maintained in due proportion.
[3.3.11] For in the same measure as the spaces between the columns increase, the thicknesses of the shafts must be enlarged in proportion.

If in the araeostyle the thickness were a ninth or a tenth part, the column will appear thin and meagre, because through the breadth of the intercolumniations the air consumes and diminishes the apparent thickness of the shafts.

Therefore one must follow the symmetries proper to the kind of work.
Moreover, the corner columns are to be made thicker by a fiftieth part of their own diameter, because they are cut around by the air and appear more slender to those looking at them.
Therefore where the eye deceives, the deficiency must be made good by calculation.

beads.greek: [3.3.12] Contracturae autem in summis columnarum hypotracheliis ita faciendae videntur, uti, si columna sit ab minimo ad pedes quinos denos, ima crassitudo dividatur in partes sex et earum partium quinque summa constituatur.
beads.english: [3.3.12] The contractions at the tops of the columns, at the hypotrachelia, seem to require the following rule. If a column is from the smallest size up to fifteen feet, let the bottom thickness be divided into six parts, and let the top thickness be set at five of those parts.

beads.greek: item quae erit ab quindecim pedibus ad pedes viginti, scapus imus in partes sex et semissem dividatur, earumque partium quinque et semisse superior crassitudo columnae fiat.
beads.english: Likewise, in a column from fifteen feet to twenty feet, let the bottom of the shaft be divided into six and a half parts, and let the upper thickness of the column be made five and a half of those parts.

beads.greek: item quae erunt a pedibus viginti ad pedes triginta, scapus imus dividatur in partes septem, earumque sex summa contractura perficiatur.
beads.english: Likewise, in columns from twenty feet to thirty feet, let the bottom of the shaft be divided into seven parts, and let the contraction at the top be completed at six of them.

beads.greek: quae autem ab triginta pedibus ad quadraginta alta erit, ima dividatur in partes septem et dimidiam; ex his sex et dimidiam in summo habeat contracturae rationem.
beads.english: A column from thirty feet to forty feet high: let its bottom be divided into seven and a half parts, and of these let it have six and a half at the top as the reckoning of its contraction.

beads.greek: quae erunt ab quadraginta pedibus ad quinquaginta, item dividendae sunt in octo partes, et earum septem in summo scapo sub capitulo contrahantur.
beads.english: Columns from forty feet to fifty feet are likewise to be divided into eight parts, and let them be contracted to seven of these at the top of the shaft, beneath the capital.

beads.greek: item si quae altiores erunt, eadem ratione pro rata constituantur contracturae.
beads.english: Likewise, if any are taller, let their contractions be determined by the same method, in proportion.

greek_sentences: [3.3.12] Contracturae autem in summis columnarum hypotracheliis ita faciendae videntur, uti, si columna sit ab minimo ad pedes quinos denos, ima crassitudo dividatur in partes sex et earum partium quinque summa constituatur.
item quae erit ab quindecim pedibus ad pedes viginti, scapus imus in partes sex et semissem dividatur, earumque partium quinque et semisse superior crassitudo columnae fiat.
item quae erunt a pedibus viginti ad pedes triginta, scapus imus dividatur in partes septem, earumque sex summa contractura perficiatur.
quae autem ab triginta pedibus ad quadraginta alta erit, ima dividatur in partes septem et dimidiam; ex his sex et dimidiam in summo habeat contracturae rationem.
quae erunt ab quadraginta pedibus ad quinquaginta, item dividendae sunt in octo partes, et earum septem in summo scapo sub capitulo contrahantur.

english_sentences: [3.3.12] The contractions at the tops of the columns, at the hypotrachelia, seem to require the following rule.
If a column is from the smallest size up to fifteen feet, let the bottom thickness be divided into six parts, and let the top thickness be set at five of those parts.

Likewise, in a column from fifteen feet to twenty feet, let the bottom of the shaft be divided into six and a half parts, and let the upper thickness of the column be made five and a half of those parts.
Likewise, in columns from twenty feet to thirty feet, let the bottom of the shaft be divided into seven parts, and let the contraction at the top be completed at six of them.
A column from thirty feet to forty feet high: let its bottom be divided into seven and a half parts, and of these let it have six and a half at the top as the reckoning of its contraction.
Columns from forty feet to fifty feet are likewise to be divided into eight parts, and let them be contracted to seven of these at the top of the shaft, beneath the capital.
Likewise, if any are taller, let their contractions be determined by the same method, in proportion.

beads.greek: [3.3.13] Haec autem propter altitudinis intervallum scandentis oculi species adiciuntur crassitudinibus temperaturae.
beads.english: [3.3.13] These tempering adjustments are added to the thicknesses on account of the interval of height over which the sight (species) of the climbing eye passes.

beads.greek: venustates enim persequitur visus, cuius si non blandimur voluptati proportione et modulorum adiectionibus, uti quod fallitur temperatione adaugeatur, vastus et invenustus conspicientibus remittetur aspectus.
beads.english: For vision pursues beauty; and if we do not gratify its pleasure by proportion and by additions of modules, so that what it is deceived about is made up by adjustment, a clumsy and ungraceful appearance will be returned to the beholders.

beads.greek: de adiectione, quae adicitur in mediis columnis, quae apud Graecos ἔντασις appellatur, in extremo libro erit forma et ratio eius, quemadmodum mollis et conveniens efficiatur, subscripta.
beads.english: Concerning the addition made at the middle of columns, which among the Greeks is called entasis, its diagram and method, showing how it may be made smooth and fitting, will be appended at the end of the book.

beads.greek: [3.4.1] Fundationes eorum operum fodiantur, si queat inveniri, ad solidum et in solido, quantum ex amplitudine operis pro ratione videbitur, extruaturque structura totum solum quam solidissima.
beads.english: [3.4.1] Let the foundations of these works be dug down to the solid and into the solid, if it can be found, as far as shall seem proportionate to the size of the work, and let the whole site be built up with masonry as solid as possible.

beads.greek: supraque terram parietes extruantur sub columnas dimidio crassiores quam columnae sunt futurae, uti firmiora sint inferiora superioribus; quae stereobates appellantur, nam excipiunt onera.
beads.english: Above ground let walls be built under the columns, thicker by one half than the columns are to be, so that the lower parts may be firmer than the upper; these are called stereobates, for they receive the loads.

beads.greek: spirarumque proiecturae non procedant extra solidum; item supra parietis ad eundem modum crassitudo servanda est.
beads.english: The projections of the bases (spirae) should not extend beyond the solid; likewise above, the thickness of the wall is to be kept in the same manner.

beads.greek: intervalla autem concamaranda aut solidanda festucationibus, uti distineantur.
beads.english: The intervals between, however, are to be vaulted over or made solid with rammed fill (festucationibus), so that they may be held apart.

beads.greek: [3.4.2] Sin autem solidum non invenietur, sed locus erit congesticius ad imum aut paluster, tunc is locus fodiatur exinaniaturque et palis alneis aut oleagineis aut robusteis ustilatis configatur, sublicaque machinis adigatur quam creberrime, carbonibusque expleantur intervalla palorum, et tunc structuris solidissimis fundamenta impleantur.
beads.english: [3.4.2] But if solid ground is not found, and the site is made-up ground down to the bottom, or marshy, then let that site be dug out and cleared, and let it be fixed with stakes of alder or of olive or of oak, charred, and let the piling be driven in by machines as closely set as possible, and let the intervals between the stakes be filled with charcoal, and then let the foundations be filled with the most solid masonry.

beads.greek: extructis autem fundamentis ad libramentum stylobatae sunt conlocandi.
beads.english: When the foundations have been built up, the stylobates are to be laid to the level.

beads.greek: [3.4.3] Supra stylobatas columnae disponendae, quemadmodum supra scriptum est, sive in pycnostylo, quemadmodum pycnostyla, sive systylo aut diastylo aut eustylo, quemadmodum supra scripta sunt et constituta.
beads.english: [3.4.3] Upon the stylobates the columns are to be arranged as has been written above, whether in the pycnostyle, in the manner of pycnostyle buildings, or in the systyle or diastyle or eustyle, as these have been described and established above.

beads.greek: in araeostylis enim libertas est quantum cuique libet constituendi.
beads.english: For in araeostyle temples there is freedom to set out the spacing as each one pleases.

beads.greek: sed ita columnae in peripteris conlocentur, uti, quot intercolumnia sunt in fronte, totidem bis intercolumnia fiant in lateribus; ita enim erit duplex longitudo operis ad latitudinem.
beads.english: But in peripteral temples let the columns be placed so that, however many intercolumniations there are on the front, twice as many intercolumniations are made on the sides; for in this way the length of the work will be double its breadth.

beads.greek: namque qui columnarum duplicationes fecerunt, erravisse videntur, quod unum intercolumnium in longitudine plus quam oporteat procurrere videtur.
beads.english: For those who have doubled the number of columns appear to have erred, because one intercolumniation seems to run on in the length further than it ought.

beads.greek: [3.4.4] Gradus in fronte constituendi ita sunt, uti sint semper inpares; namque cum dextro pede primus gradus ascendatur, item in summo templo primus erit ponendus.
beads.english: [3.4.4] The steps at the front are to be arranged so that they are always odd in number; for since the first step is ascended with the right foot, the right foot will likewise have to be set down first at the top of the temple.

beads.greek: crassitudines autem eorum graduum ita finiendas censeo, ut neque crassiores dextante nec tenuiores dodrante sint conlocatae; sic enim durus non erit ascensus.
beads.english: The thicknesses of these steps I consider should be so limited that they are set neither thicker than a dextans nor thinner than a dodrans; for in this way the ascent will not be hard.

beads.greek: retractiones autem graduum nec minus quam sesquipedales nec plus quam bipedales faciendae videntur.
beads.english: The treads of the steps, it seems, should be made not less than a foot and a half nor more than two feet.

beads.greek: item si circa aedem gradus futuri sunt, ad eundem modum fieri debent.
beads.english: Likewise, if there are to be steps around the temple, they ought to be made in the same manner.

beads.greek: [3.4.5] Sin autem circa aedem ex tribus lateribus podium faciendum erit, id constituatur, uti quadrae, spirae, trunci, coronae, lysis ad ipsum stylobatam, qui erit sub columnarum spiris, conveniant.
beads.english: [3.4.5] But if a podium is to be made around the temple on three sides, it should be so constructed that the plinths, bases, dies, cornices and lysis correspond to the stylobate itself, which will be under the bases of the columns.

beads.greek: stylobatam ita oportet exaequari, uti habeat per medium adiectionem per scamillos inpares; si enim ad libellam dirigetur, alveolatum oculo videbitur.
beads.english: The stylobate must be levelled in such a way that it has an addition along the middle by means of unequal scamilli; for if it is laid out to the level, it will appear to the eye hollowed like a trough.

beads.greek: hoc autem, ut scamilli ad id convenientes fiant, item in extremo libro forma et demonstratio erit descripta.
beads.english: How the scamilli may be made to suit this purpose will likewise be set out, with a diagram and demonstration, at the end of the book.

beads.greek: [3.5.1] His perfectis in suis locis spirae conlocentur, eaeque ad symmetriam sic perficiantur, uti crassitudo cum plintho sit columnae ex dimidia crassitudine proiecturamque, quam Graeci ἐκφοράν vocitant, habeant S extantem: ita tum lata et longa erit columnae crassitudinis unius et dimidiae.
beads.english: [3.5.1] When these things have been completed, let the bases be set in their places, and let them be finished according to symmetry in such a way that their thickness, together with the plinth, is half the thickness of the column, and that they have a projection, which the Greeks call ἐκφορά, of a sixth (reading the transmitted 'S extantem' as 'sextantem'); thus the base will then be one and a half thicknesses of the column in breadth and in length.

beads.greek: [3.5.2] Altitudo eius, si atticurges erit, ita dividatur, ut superior pars tertia parte sit crassitudinis columnae, reliquum plintho relinquatur.
beads.english: [3.5.2] Its height, if it is to be of the Attic type, is to be divided so that the upper part is a third part of the thickness of the column, and the remainder is left to the plinth.

beads.greek: dempta plintho reliquum dividatur in partes quattuor, fiatque superior torus quartae; reliquae tres aequaliter dividantur, et una sit inferior torus, altera pars cum suis quadris scotia, quam Graeci τροχίλον dicunt.
beads.english: With the plinth taken away, let the remainder be divided into four parts, and let the upper torus be made of a fourth; let the remaining three be divided equally, and let one part be the lower torus, and the other part, together with its fillets, the scotia, which the Greeks call τροχίλος.

beads.greek: [3.5.3] Sin autem ionicae erunt faciendae, symmetriae earum sic erunt constituendae, uti latitudo spirae quoqueversus sit columnae crassitudinis adiecta e crassitudine quarta et octava.
beads.english: [3.5.3] But if Ionic bases are to be made, their symmetries are to be so established that the breadth of the base in every direction is the thickness of the column, with a fourth and an eighth of the thickness added to it.

beads.greek: altitudo ita uti atticurges; item et eius plinthos; reliquumque praeter plinthum, quod erit tertia pars crassitudinis columnae, dividatur in partes septem: inde trium partium torus, qui est in summo; reliquae quattuor partes dividendae sunt aequaliter, et una pars fiat cum suis astragalis et supercilio superior trochilus, altera pars inferiori trochilo relinquatur; sed inferior maior apparebit, ideo quod habebit ad extremam plinthum proiecturam.
beads.english: The height is to be as in the Attic type, and likewise its plinth; and let the remainder apart from the plinth, which will be a third part of the thickness of the column, be divided into seven parts: of these, three parts go to the torus which is at the top; the remaining four parts are to be divided equally, and let one part, together with its astragals and the overhanging fillet, form the upper trochilus, and let the other part be left to the lower trochilus; but the lower will appear larger, because it will have a projection out to the edge of the plinth.

beads.greek: astragali faciendi sunt octavae partis trochili.
beads.english: The astragals are to be made of an eighth part of the trochilus.

beads.greek: proiectura erit spirae pars octava et sexta decuma pars crassitudinis columnae.
beads.english: The projection of the base will be an eighth and a sixteenth part of the thickness of the column.

beads.greek: [3.5.4] Spiris perfectis et conlocatis columnae sunt medianae in pronao et postico ad perpendiculum medii centri conlocandae, angulares autem quaeque e regione earum futurae sunt in lateribus aedis dextra ac sinistra, uti partes interiores, quae ad parietes cellae spectant, ad perpendiculum latus habeant conlocatum, exteriores autem partes †uti dicant se earum contracturam.
beads.english: [3.5.4] When the bases have been finished and set in place, the middle columns in the pronaos and in the posticum are to be set up on the perpendicular of their middle centre; but the corner columns, and those which are to stand in line with them on the sides of the temple, right and left, are to be so set that their inner parts, which face the walls of the cella, have their side set on the perpendicular, while their outer parts †uti dicant se† (text corrupt: apparently, 'show/carry') their diminution (contractura).

beads.greek: sic enim erunt figurae compositionis aedium contractura eius tali ratione exactae.
beads.english: For in this way the figures of the composition of temples will be brought to completion by a diminution made on this principle.

beads.greek: [3.5.5] Scapis columnarum statutis capitulorum ratio sic est habenda.
beads.english: [3.5.5] When the shafts of the columns have been set up, the principle of the capitals is to be handled as follows.

beads.greek: si pulvinata erunt, his symmetriis conformabuntur, uti, quam crassus imus scapus fuerit addita octava decuma parte scapi, abacus habeat longitudinem et latitudinem; crassitudinem cum volutis eius dimidiam.
beads.english: If they are to be cushion-shaped (pulvinata), they will be formed in these symmetries: the abacus is to have as its length and breadth the thickness of the bottom of the shaft with an eighteenth part of the shaft added; its thickness, together with the volutes, is to be half of this.

beads.greek: recedendum autem est ab extremo abaco in interiorem partem frontibus volutarum parte duodevicensima et eius dimidia.
beads.english: One must draw back from the edge of the abacus towards the inside, for the faces of the volutes, by an eighteenth part and the half of that.

beads.greek: tunc crassitudo dividenda est in partes novem et dimidiam, et secundum abacum in quattuor partibus volutarum secundum extremi abaci quadram lineae demittendae, quae cathetoe dicuntur.
beads.english: Then the thickness is to be divided into nine and a half parts, and along the abacus, at the four sides of the volutes, lines are to be let fall along the fillet (quadra) at the edge of the abacus; these are called cathetoe.

beads.greek: tunc ex novem partibus et dimidia una pars et dimidia abaci crassitudo relinquatur, reliquae octo volutis constituantur.
beads.english: Then of the nine and a half parts let one part and a half be left for the thickness of the abacus, and let the remaining eight be assigned to the volutes.

english_sentences: [3.5.4] When the bases have been finished and set in place, the middle columns in the pronaos and in the posticum are to be set up on the perpendicular of their middle centre; but the corner columns, and those which are to stand in line with them on the sides of the temple, right and left, are to be so set that their inner parts, which face the walls of the cella, have their side set on the perpendicular, while their outer parts †uti dicant se† (text corrupt: apparently, 'show/carry') their diminution (contractura).
For in this way the figures of the composition of temples will be brought to completion by a diminution made on this principle.
[3.5.5] When the shafts of the columns have been set up, the principle of the capitals is to be handled as follows.

If they are to be cushion-shaped (pulvinata), they will be formed in these symmetries: the abacus is to have as its length and breadth the thickness of the bottom of the shaft with an eighteenth part of the shaft added; its thickness, together with the volutes, is to be half of this.
One must draw back from the edge of the abacus towards the inside, for the faces of the volutes, by an eighteenth part and the half of that.

Then the thickness is to be divided into nine and a half parts, and along the abacus, at the four sides of the volutes, lines are to be let fall along the fillet (quadra) at the edge of the abacus; these are called cathetoe.
Then of the nine and a half parts let one part and a half be left for the thickness of the abacus, and let the remaining eight be assigned to the volutes.

beads.greek: [3.5.6] Tunc ab linea, quae secundum abaci extremam partem demissa erit, in interiorem partem alia recedat unius et dimidiatae partis latitudine.
beads.english: [3.5.6] Then from the line which will have been let fall along the outer edge of the abacus, another line is to recede towards the inner side by a breadth of one and a half parts.

beads.greek: deinde hae lineae dividantur ita, ut quattuor partes et dimidia sub abaco relinquantur.
beads.english: Next these lines are to be divided so that four and a half parts are left below the abacus.

beads.greek: tunc in eo loco, qui locus dividit quattuor et dimidiam et tres et dimidiam partem, centrum oculi conlocetur signeturque ex eo centro rotunda circinatio tam magna in diametro, quam una pars ex octo partibus est.
beads.english: Then at the point which divides the four and a half parts from the three and a half parts, the centre of the eye is to be placed, and from that centre a round compass-drawn circle is to be described, as great in diameter as one part out of the eight parts.

beads.greek: ea erit oculi magnitudine, et in ea catheto respondens diametros agatur.
beads.english: This will be of the size of the eye, and in it a diameter corresponding to the cathetus is to be drawn.

beads.greek: tunc ab summo sub abaco inceptum schema volutae in singulis tetrantorum actionibus dimidiatum oculi spatium minuatur, doneque in eundem tetrantem, qui subest, conveniat.
beads.english: Then, starting from the top beneath the abacus, the figure of the volute is to be diminished, in each of the turnings through the quadrants, by half the space of the eye, until it comes round into that same quadrant which lies beneath.

beads.greek: [3.5.7] Capituli autem crassitudo sic est facienda, ut ex novem partibus et dimidia tres partes praependeant infra astragalum summi scapi; cymatio, adempto abaco et canali, reliqua sit pars.
beads.english: [3.5.7] The depth of the capital is to be made thus: of the nine and a half parts, three parts are to hang down below the astragal at the top of the shaft; the remaining part is to go to the cymatium, once the abacus and the channel have been taken away.

beads.greek: proiectura autem cymatii habeat extra abaci quadram oculi magnitudinem.
beads.english: The projection of the cymatium beyond the square of the abacus is to be the size of the eye.

beads.greek: pulvinorum baltei ab abaco hanc habeant proiecturam, uti circini centrum unum cum sit positum in capituli tetrante et alterum diducatur ad extremum cymatium, circumactum balteorum extremas partes tangat.
beads.english: The belts of the cushions are to have this projection from the abacus: when one point of a pair of compasses has been placed in the quadrant of the capital and the other is drawn out to the outer edge of the cymatium, the compasses, when swung round, should touch the outermost parts of the belts.

beads.greek: axes volutarum ne crassiores sint quam oculi magnitudo, volutaeque ipsae succidantur altitudinis suae duodecimam partem.
beads.english: The axes of the volutes are not to be thicker than the size of the eye, and the volutes themselves are to be cut in by a twelfth part of their height.

beads.greek: haec erunt symmetriae capitulorum, quae columnae futurae sunt ab minimo ad pedes XXV .
beads.english: These will be the symmetries of the capitals for columns that are to be from the smallest size up to 25 feet.

beads.greek: quae supra erunt, reliqua habebunt ad eundem modum symmetrias, abacus autem erit longus et latus, quam crassa columna est ima adiecta parte VIIII , uti, quo minus habuerit altior columna contractum, eo ne minus habeat capitulum suae symmetriae proiecturam et in latitudine suae partis adiectionem.
beads.english: Columns above that will have their other symmetries in the same manner, but the abacus will be as long and as broad as the column is thick at the bottom, with a ninth part added. The purpose is that, although the taller column has less contraction, the capital should not on that account have any less of the projection proper to its symmetry, or of the addition of its due part in breadth.

beads.english: [3.5.8] Concerning the drawing of the volutes, namely how they are to be described so that they may be correctly coiled with the pair of compasses, their figure and method will be set out at the end of the book.

beads.greek: [3.5.8] De volutarum descriptionibus, uti ad circinum sint recte involutae, quemadmodum describantur, in extremo libro forma et ratio earum erit subscripta.
beads.english: When the capitals have been completed and then set on the shafts of the columns, not by the level but according to a uniform module, so that whatever addition has been made in the stylobates may correspond in the upper members, the method of the architraves is to be as follows. If the columns are from a minimum of twelve feet up to fifteen feet, the height of the architrave should be half the thickness of the column at the bottom.

beads.greek: Capitulis perfectis, deinde in scapis columnarum non ad libellam sed ad aequalem modulum conlocatis, ut, quae adiectio in stylobatis facta fuerit, in superioribus membris respondeat , epistyliorum ratio sic est habenda, uti, si columnae fuerint a minima XII pedum ad quindecim pedes, epistylii sit altitudo dimidia crassitudinis imae columnae; item si ab XV pedibus ad XX , columnae altitudo dimetiatur in partes tredecim, et unius partis altitudo epistylii fiat; item si XX ad XXV pedes, dividatur altitudo in partes XII et semissem, et eius una pars epistylium in altitudine fiat; item si ab XXV pedibus ad XXX , dividatur in partes XII , et eius una pars altitudo fiat.
beads.english: Likewise, if from fifteen feet to twenty, let the height of the column be measured off into thirteen parts, and let the height of the architrave be made one part. Likewise, if from twenty to twenty-five feet, let the height be divided into twelve parts and a half, and let one part of it be made the architrave in height.

beads.greek: item si quae altiores erunt, rata parte ad eundem modum ex altitudine columnarum expediendae sunt altitudines epistyliorum.
beads.english: Likewise, if from twenty-five feet to thirty, let it be divided into twelve parts, and let one part of it be made the height. Likewise, if any are taller, the heights of the architraves are to be worked out from the height of the columns in the same manner, in due proportion.

When the capitals have been completed and then set on the shafts of the columns, not by the level but according to a uniform module, so that whatever addition has been made in the stylobates may correspond in the upper members, the method of the architraves is to be as follows.
If the columns are from a minimum of twelve feet up to fifteen feet, the height of the architrave should be half the thickness of the column at the bottom.
Likewise, if from fifteen feet to twenty, let the height of the column be measured off into thirteen parts, and let the height of the architrave be made one part.
Likewise, if from twenty to twenty-five feet, let the height be divided into twelve parts and a half, and let one part of it be made the architrave in height.
Likewise, if from twenty-five feet to thirty, let it be divided into twelve parts, and let one part of it be made the height.
Likewise, if any are taller, the heights of the architraves are to be worked out from the height of the columns in the same manner, in due proportion.

beads.greek: [3.5.9] Quo altius enim scandit oculi species, non facile persecat aeris crebritatem; dilapsa itaque altitudinis spatio et viribus exuta incertam modulorum renuntiat sensibus quantitatem.
beads.english: [3.5.9] For the higher the sight of the eye climbs, the less easily does it cut through the density of the air; and so, having dispersed over the extent of the height and been stripped of its strength, it reports to the senses an uncertain quantity of the modules.

beads.greek: quare semper adiciendum est rationis supplementum in symmetriarum membris, ut, cum fuerint aut altioribus locis opera aut etiam ipsa colossicotera, habeant magnitudinum rationem.
beads.english: Therefore a supplement by calculation must always be added in the members of the symmetries, so that, when works are either in higher places or are themselves of more colossal size, they may keep a due proportion of magnitudes.

beads.greek: epistylii latitudo in imo, quod supra capitulum erit, quanta crassitudo summae columnae sub capitulo erit, tanta fiat; summum, quantum imus scapus.
beads.english: The breadth of the architrave at the bottom, where it will lie above the capital, is to be made as great as the thickness of the top of the column beneath the capital will be; at the top, as great as the bottom of the shaft.

beads.greek: [3.5.10] Cymatium epistylii septima parte suae altitudinis est faciendum, et in proiectura tantundem.
beads.english: [3.5.10] The cymatium of the architrave is to be made a seventh part of its height, and the same amount in projection.

beads.greek: reliqua pars praeter cymatium dividenda est in partes XII , et earum trium ima fascia est facienda, secunda IIII , summa V .
beads.english: The remaining part, apart from the cymatium, is to be divided into twelve parts, and the lowest fascia is to be made of three of these, the second of four, the topmost of five.

beads.greek: item zophorus supra epistylium quarta parte minus altus quam epistylium; sin autem sigilla designari oportuerit, quarta parte altior quam epistylium, uti auctoritatem habeant scalpturae.
beads.english: Likewise the frieze (zophorus) above the architrave is to be a fourth part less high than the architrave; but if figures are to be represented on it, a fourth part higher than the architrave, so that the carvings may have impressiveness.

beads.greek: cymatium suae altitudinis partis septimae; proiecturae cymatiûm quantum crassitudo.
beads.english: Its cymatium is to be a seventh part of its height; the projection of the cymatia is to be as much as their thickness.
